chapters.title: Playing Pilgrims
chapters.intro: Background on The Pilgrim’s Progress, the Civil War home front and 1860s family life, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: A scornful word for a cheeky or silly young girl.
A neat, stiff-petaled garden flower; “prim as a China-aster” means very stiff and proper.
A pair of small hollow wooden shells clicked together in the hand, used in Spanish dance music.
A white-flowered plant (a hellebore) that blooms in the middle of winter.
An alcove or hollow set back into a wall, often holding shelves.
Rigid and awkward; a poker is the iron rod used to stir a fire.
An actor famous for playing tragic roles, or a writer of tragedies.
A woman’s hat tied under the chin, usually framing the face.
Called up by law for compulsory military service.
A minister attached to an army regiment, hospital or similar body, who leads worship and comforts the sick and dying.
A bag for keeping scraps of fabric saved for patching and sewing.
A bog or swamp; figuratively, a state of hopeless gloom.
Thoughtful in a quiet, slightly sad way.

An allegory by the English Puritan preacher John Bunyan, published in 1678 and for two centuries one of the most widely read books in English homes after the Bible. Its hero, Christian, carries a heavy burden on his back and journeys from the City of Destruction to the Celestial City, which stands for heaven.

On his way Christian falls into the Slough of Despond (a bog of despair) and is pulled out by a man named Help; he must fight Apollyon, a winged demon, and pass through a dark valley full of hobgoblins. He also carries a roll, or scroll, that guides and reassures him.

Two romantic tales by the German writer Friedrich de la Motte Fouqué, often printed together in English. Undine is the story of a water spirit who marries a knight; Sintram is a darker tale of a knight struggling against temptation.

Shakespeare’s tragedy of a Scottish nobleman who murders his king. Its famous lines include Macbeth’s vision of a floating dagger, and the ghost of his murdered friend Banquo appears at a feast; in theaters, ghosts often rose through a trapdoor in the stage.
A line from a moral verse for children by the hymn writer Isaac Watts, urging brothers and sisters not to quarrel.

The American Civil War (1861–65) was fought between the Northern states (the Union) and the Southern states that had seceded (the Confederacy). Families in New England sent husbands and sons far south, often for years, and waited anxiously for letters.
From 1863 the Union drafted men aged 20 to 45. A drafted man could hire a substitute or, for a time, pay $300 to be excused.
Women attached to some regiments, a custom borrowed from the French army, who sold food and drink to soldiers, wore a version of the uniform and sometimes nursed the wounded.
Women and girls at home knitted socks and mittens, sewed shirts and packed boxes of supplies for the army, often through local aid societies.

Respectable families who had lost their money often kept their manners, books and education while doing without servants, new clothes and luxuries. Daughters might take work as teachers, governesses or companions to older ladies.
A German firm, Faber, made high-quality drawing pencils that were prized by artists and students in the 19th century.
Before radio and film, families staged plays at home with homemade costumes and scenery. Melodramas with villains, witches, potions and rescued heroines were favorites.
The nursery song comes from a poem by the English writer Jane Taylor, first published in 1806.

quiz.q: What does Jo want to buy for herself with her dollar?
o: Some new sheet music
A box of Faber’s drawing-pencils
A copy of Undine and Sintram
A new pair of gloves
quiz.e: Jo, “who was a bookworm,” has wanted Undine and Sintram for a long time; Beth had planned on music and Amy on Faber’s pencils.

quiz.q: Which sister does Father call “Little Tranquillity”?
o: Elizabeth
Margaret
Josephine
Amy
quiz.e: Thirteen-year-old Elizabeth, called Beth, is shy and peaceful and “seemed to live in a happy world of her own.”

quiz.q: What do the girls decide to do with their dollars?
o: Send it to the soldiers in Father’s regiment
Save it to buy Father a gift for his return
Spend it on costumes and props for the Christmas play
Buy Marmee gifts instead of things for themselves
quiz.e: Prompted by Marmee’s worn slippers, Beth suggests it: Meg will give gloves, Jo army shoes, Beth handkerchiefs and Amy cologne.

quiz.q: Why was Amy given a part in Jo’s play?
o: She is the best singer of the four sisters
She is small enough for the villain to carry off
She begged Jo for a part with a fainting scene
She is the only one who can play the witch
quiz.e: Amy “was not gifted with dramatic power,” and her fainting scene in rehearsal is hopelessly stiff.

quiz.q: In what role has Mr. March gone to the war?
o: Chaplain
Army surgeon
Drummer
Quartermaster
quiz.e: Meg admires him for going as a chaplain “when he was too old to be drafted, and not strong enough for a soldier.”

quiz.q: What does Father’s letter call the girls at its close?
o: his brave soldiers
his four pilgrims
his little women
his good daughters
quiz.e: He hopes they will “conquer themselves so beautifully” that he will be prouder than ever “of my little women.”

quiz.q: When Mrs. March thinks Beth has no burden, what does Beth name?
o: Her rough hands and an old piano that won’t stay in tune
Dishes and dusters, envy of nice pianos, and her shyness
Missing Father and fearing he will never come home
Sharing a room and old dolls with her younger sister
quiz.e: Beth’s bundle is “dishes and dusters, and envying girls with nice pianos, and being afraid of people.” Nobody laughs, so as not to hurt her.

quiz.q: How do the girls make the dull sewing of Aunt March’s sheets go faster?
o: Beth plays the piano while the others sew
They take turns reading aloud from Bunyan
They race one another to the end of each seam
They call the quarters of each seam continents
quiz.e: Following Jo’s plan, the quarters are Europe, Asia, Africa and America, and they talk about each country as they stitch through it.

chapters.title: A Merry Christmas
chapters.intro: Background on 1860s Christmas customs, immigrant poverty, homemade melodrama and holiday treats, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: A dialect word for food and provisions (from “victuals”).
Dialect for fuel, such as wood or coal for the fire.
Old slang for a thoroughly good, generous, dependable person.
Pancakes made from buckwheat flour, a common breakfast.
A thin porridge of oatmeal or other meal boiled in water or milk, often given to the sick.
A small boat-shaped jug for serving melted butter or sauce.
Small pieces of shiny metal sewn onto clothing to make it glitter; sequins.
A light, blunt-tipped sword used in fencing.
A close-fitting padded jacket worn by men in Europe from about the 14th to the 17th century. “Slashed” doublets had decorative cuts showing a different fabric beneath.
In a theater, the first raised tier of seats above the main floor, once the most fashionable place to sit.
Printed cotton cloth, usually with a flowered pattern, used for curtains and covers.
A thick woolen cloth, usually green, used for tabletops and coverings.
A folding wooden frame for drying or airing clothes indoors.
Mysterious and occult, like secret magical symbols.
A magic potion, especially one meant to make someone fall in love.
A window made of small panes set in a crisscross frame.
Fancy sweets, often of sugar or chocolate, especially French ones.

Hanging stockings by the fireplace for St. Nicholas to fill was an established American custom. The poem “A Visit from St. Nicholas” (1823) did much to fix the image of Santa Claus, and in the early 1860s the cartoonist Thomas Nast began drawing him for Harper’s Weekly.
Christmas presents in ordinary homes were usually few and often handmade: hemmed handkerchiefs, knitted or sewn items, a book or a little ornament.
Christmas was a traditional time for the comfortably off to bring food, fuel and clothing to poor neighbors. Middle-class women commonly visited the poor in person.
Large numbers of Germans emigrated to the United States in the 1840s and 1850s. Many newcomers lived in great poverty in crowded rooms, spoke little English and took whatever work they could find.
“Ach, mein Gott!” means “Oh, my God!”; “Das ist gut” means “That is good”; “Engel” means “angel” and “Kinder” means “children.”
Many middle-class families kept at least one servant who cooked and cleaned. A long-serving servant could become almost one of the family, speaking freely and sharing its joys and troubles.

A popular kind of play with a sneering villain, a persecuted heroine, a brave lover, a stern father and plenty of songs, potions, fights and sudden rescues. Amateur versions used homemade scenery and costumes.
Ice cream was a special treat. It was made with ice cut from frozen ponds in winter and stored in icehouses, and churned by hand in a crank freezer, a device patented in America in 1843.
Fresh flowers in midwinter came from heated glasshouses and were an expensive luxury.

quiz.q: What does each sister find under her pillow on Christmas morning?
o: A letter Father wrote for Christmas
A little book, each a different color
A pair of mittens knitted by Marmee
A dollar and a note from Aunt March
quiz.e: Marmee’s promised “guidebook”: four little books with the same picture inside and a few words from their mother, telling “the best life ever lived.”

quiz.q: What has Beth marked on the handkerchiefs for Marmee?
o: “M. March”
“Marmee”
“Mother”
quiz.e: Beth chose “Mother” because Meg’s initials are also M. M., and she wants no one but Marmee to use them.

quiz.q: Why did Amy go out early on Christmas morning?
o: To trade the small cologne for a bigger bottle
To pick a rose to trim Marmee’s bouquet
To fetch Marmee’s new slippers from the shop
To buy candy for the audience at the play
quiz.e: After reading and talking about being good, Amy felt ashamed of her cheap present and spent all her money on a handsome flask.

quiz.q: What does Mrs. March ask the girls to give the poor family?
o: Their own Christmas presents
Their pocket money
Their Christmas breakfast
Their winter cloaks
quiz.e: A poor mother with a newborn and six hungry children has no food or fire; the girls carry over their breakfast and make do with bread and milk.

quiz.q: What do the hungry Hummel children call the girls?
o: Christmas fairies
Little saints
Kind neighbors
Angel children
quiz.e: They cry “Die Engel-kinder!” Jo jokes that they are “funny angels in hoods and mittens.”

quiz.q: What goes wrong in the tower scene of the play?
o: Hugo’s sword catches in the curtains and pulls them down
Zara’s train catches and the tower falls on the lovers
The rope-ladder snaps as Zara begins to climb down
The witch’s furnace sets the cave of bureaus alight
quiz.e: The tower totters and buries Zara and Roderigo, and Amy’s golden head pops out crying “I told you so!” while Don Pedro hisses “Act as if it was all right!”

quiz.q: What ends the applause at the close of the play?
o: The cot-bed they sit on suddenly folds shut
Hannah stops the play because of the noise
The lamp smokes so badly that they all leave
A spark from the furnace singes the curtains
quiz.e: The cot-bed holding the “dress-circle” shuts up and “extinguished the enthusiastic audience,” though all are pulled out unhurt.

quiz.q: Who sent the splendid supper of ice cream, cake and flowers?
o: Aunt March
Mrs. March herself
Old Mr. Laurence
The King family
quiz.e: Hannah had told one of his servants about the breakfast. He knew Mrs. March’s father years ago, and Jo is sure his grandson put the idea into his head.

chapters.title: The Laurence Boy
chapters.intro: Background on Victorian novels, party dress and grooming, dances and parlor games, and schooling abroad, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: A room or attic space right under the roof of a house.
A kind of apple with rough, brownish skin.
A thick quilt; also a long woolen scarf.
A ribbed fabric, often of silk and wool or cotton, cheaper than pure silk.
To leap and frolic about playfully.
The business of dressing, arranging the hair and getting ready; also a person’s outfit.
A band or net worn to hold back a woman’s hair.
To primp; to fuss over one’s appearance in a mirror.
Light, low shoes without fastenings, worn by men for dancing.
A lively dance for couples that began in Bohemia and swept Europe and America in the 1840s.
Rubber overshoes worn over ordinary shoes in wet weather.
An old short gun with a flared muzzle; also a clumsy, blundering person.
A Bohemian couple dance in triple time, somewhat like a waltz.
A herbal remedy, made from a mountain flower, rubbed on bruises and sprains.
A novel by the English writer Charlotte M. Yonge, published in 1853 and enormously popular. Its high-minded, passionate hero and its sorrowful turns made generations of readers weep.
A saying from the Bible’s Book of Exodus, where one of the plagues sent on Egypt is a thick darkness covering the land for three days.
A well-dressed lady at a party wore clean gloves, usually of light-colored kid leather. Bare or stained hands were thought careless, and gloves were costly to replace.
A silk dress was the mark of a grown-up, well-off young lady. Girls of modest means wore cheaper fabrics such as poplin and kept one good dress for parties.
To make ringlets, hair was wound around twists of paper and then pressed with tongs heated in the fire.
Even a small dance began with a written note in the third person (“Mrs. … would be happy to see Miss …”), and the proper reply was a note to “accept with thanks.”
Young ladies went to evening parties in pairs or with an escort, and a servant or relative was usually sent to fetch them home at an agreed hour.

Parties often ended with bonbons and “mottoes,” sweets wrapped in paper printed with a verse. “Buzz” was a counting game in which players say “buzz” instead of any number containing or divisible by seven.

Rich families sometimes sent sons to boarding schools in Switzerland, many of them around Lake Geneva at towns such as Vevey (once spelled Vevay), where lessons were in French. Heidelberg, in Germany, had a famous old university known for student clubs and festivities.
Proper young ladies were taught to take short steps, sit still, avoid staring and avoid boyish slang. Whistling, striding and blunt talk were considered unladylike.

quiz.q: What is Jo doing when Meg brings the invitation?
o: Writing a new play in the parlor
Skating on the river with some boys
Reading to Aunt March in her library
Crying over a novel in the garret
quiz.e: Jo is wrapped in a comforter in the garret, eating apples and crying over The Heir of Redclyffe, with her pet rat Scrabble nearby.

quiz.q: How do the sisters solve the problem of Jo’s stained gloves?
o: Jo borrows Marmee’s second-best pair of gloves
Each wears one good glove and holds a bad one
Jo keeps her hands behind her back all night
Jo goes without gloves and refuses to dance
quiz.e: It is Jo’s idea; Meg worries Jo’s bigger hand will stretch her glove, but lends it.

quiz.q: What goes wrong as Jo dresses Meg’s hair?
o: Her ribbon catches fire from the candle
Amy spills the curling-water over it
The hot tongs scorch off the papered locks
Her hair comes out straighter than before
quiz.e: The hair comes away with the papers, leaving “a row of little scorched bundles”; Amy suggests a ribbon over the frizzle.

quiz.q: Where does Jo first meet the Laurence boy at the party?
o: In a curtained recess where both are hiding
On the stairs while waiting for the supper
In the dressing-room while fixing her collar
Beside the punch table while fetching coffee
quiz.e: Fleeing a redheaded youth she feared would ask her to dance, Jo slips into a recess and finds that “another bashful person had chosen the same refuge.”

quiz.q: Why does Theodore Laurence go by “Laurie”?
o: It was what his teachers called him at Vevay
The fellows at school called him “Dora”
His grandfather is also named Theodore
He thinks Theodore sounds too old-fashioned
quiz.e: He made the boys stop calling him Dora by thrashing them. Jo likewise hates “Josephine.”

quiz.q: How old is Laurie?
o: Seventeen already
Fourteen and a half
Eighteen next spring
Sixteen next month
quiz.e: Jo had imagined him seventeen; he says he won’t go to college before seventeen, and he hates the idea.

quiz.q: What happens to Meg during the party?
o: She tears her best lace frill dancing
She loses Marmee’s little pearl pin
She sprains her ankle in her tight slippers
She faints from the heat of the crowded room
quiz.e: Her “stupid high heel turned”; she hides the injury and waits for Hannah rather than pay for a carriage.

quiz.q: How do the girls get home from the party?
o: In Mr. Laurence’s carriage, with Laurie on the box
In a hired carriage that Jo pays for herself
On foot, with Hannah helping Meg along
In the Gardiners’ carriage with Sallie’s friends
quiz.e: Laurie insists he always leaves early and that it is on his way; he rides on the box so Meg can keep her foot up.

chapters.title: Burdens
chapters.intro: Background on the books and stories the characters mention, work for genteel young women, 1860s schools and wartime relief work, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: To work very hard and wearily; drudgery.
A small pie made by folding pastry over a filling and baking it.
Spoiled or withered; ruined by misfortune.
A woman employed in a private home to look after and teach young children.
Of a young woman: formally introduced into adult society, so she could attend balls and receive suitors.
A sculpture of a person’s head, shoulders and chest.
Weak or frail through age or illness.
A bucket or scuttle for carrying coal to the fire.
A straight nose that continues the line of the forehead, as in classical Greek statues; long considered the ideal.
A drawing that exaggerates someone’s features to make fun of them.
The way a person carries and conducts herself; good manners and posture.
A trusted person with whom one shares secrets and private thoughts.
A reddish-orange semi-precious stone, often set in rings.
The Old Man of the Sea

In the Arabian Nights tale of Sinbad the Sailor, an old man begs Sinbad to carry him on his shoulders, then clamps his legs around his neck and refuses to get off. The phrase came to mean a burden or person one cannot shake off.
A collection of serious essays on philosophy, history and literature by the English writer William Belsham, worthy but notoriously dull reading.
A comic, warm-hearted novel by Oliver Goldsmith (1766) about a kindly country clergyman, Dr. Primrose, and the misfortunes of his family.
Harriet Beecher Stowe’s antislavery novel (1852), the best-selling novel of the century in America. Aunt Chloe, the wife of the enslaved hero Tom, is a cook whose speech is written in dialect.
Raphael (1483–1520), the Italian Renaissance painter famous for graceful Madonnas; a by-word for artistic talent.
Daughters of a respectable family that had come down in the world could earn money in only a few “ladylike” ways: as a governess, a teacher, or a paid companion to an elderly lady.
A childless, wealthy relative’s will could make or break a family’s fortunes, so poorer relations were expected to keep on good terms with them.
During the Civil War, women across the North formed aid societies that met in rented rooms to cut and sew clothing, roll bandages and pack supplies for soldiers and army hospitals.
Washington, D.C., became one great hospital during the war, with tens of thousands of sick and wounded soldiers in converted buildings and new hospital camps.
Pupils did sums and lessons on small framed slates with a slate pencil, wiping them clean to reuse; paper was saved for copybooks.
Teachers punished pupils openly: standing on the platform in front of the class, being led by the ear, or rapped on the hand with a ruler were all common.

quiz.q: Whom does Jo compare Aunt March to?
o: The Old Man of the Sea
A dragon in a fairy tale
The giant in Jack’s beanstalk
The witch in one of her plays
quiz.e: Jo hopes that when she has learned to carry her “without complaining,” Aunt March will tumble off or grow light.

quiz.q: How did the March family lose its money?
o: A bank failed in the first year of the war
Aunt March kept back an inheritance
Mr. March lost it trying to help a friend
Mr. March gave it all to the Union army
quiz.e: After the loss, Meg and Jo begged to help support the family; Meg became a nursery governess at the Kings’ and Jo a companion to Aunt March.

quiz.q: What really keeps Jo happy at Aunt March’s?
o: She is paid more than Meg is at the Kings’
Uncle March’s old library of fine books
Aunt March lets her write in the afternoons
She can ride Aunt March’s carriage horses
quiz.e: While Aunt March naps, Jo curls up in the dusty library and devours books until the shrill call of “Josy-phine!”

quiz.q: Why does Beth not go to school?
o: She is needed to help Hannah at home
She has been ill since she was small
Her parents cannot afford the fees
She is too bashful and suffered there
quiz.e: School was tried but given up; she studied with her father and keeps on alone now that he is away.

quiz.q: What does Amy call the greatest trial of her life?
o: Her cousin’s clothes
Her sums
Her nose
Mr. Davis
quiz.e: Jo once dropped baby Amy into the coal-hod, and Amy is sure the fall ruined her nose; she longs for a Grecian one.

quiz.q: In Amy’s story, how is Susie Perkins punished?
o: She stands on the platform holding her slate
She is sent home and her ring is taken away
She has to write lines all the afternoon
She is rapped on the hands with a ruler
quiz.e: Mr. Davis caught her caricature of him, led her by the ear to the platform and made her stand there half an hour holding the slate.

quiz.q: What did Beth see Mr. Laurence do at the fish-shop?
o: Pay a poor woman’s bill at the counter for her
Scold Mr. Cutter for turning a woman away
Buy oysters to send to the Hummel children
Give a hungry woman a fish with his cane
quiz.e: He hooked up a big fish with his cane for a woman who had offered to scrub in exchange for food; she hurried off hugging it.

quiz.q: In Marmee’s fable, what does the old woman advise the four girls?
o: Work hard every day and never envy the rich
Think over your blessings and be grateful
Give away what you most want to keep
Pray each night for the things you lack
quiz.e: The story turns the girls’ own tales into lessons; Meg protests that Marmee gave them “a sermon instead of a romance.”

chapters.title: Being Neighborly
chapters.intro: Background on Ivanhoe and The Pilgrim’s Progress, neighborly visiting customs, wealthy households and sickroom fare, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: A loose, unfitted jacket or short coat.
To be a sign of; to indicate.
A building for keeping a carriage, often beside the stables.
A glass-walled room or greenhouse, often heated, for growing plants and flowers.
To set out boldly, as soldiers rushing out of a fortress.
An old, humorous word for the top of the head.
A sweet, smooth molded pudding of milk or cream set with cornstarch or gelatin.
To court someone in the hope of marrying them.
A deep, softly upholstered armchair that invites one to doze.
Formidable; a person to be respected or feared.
Here, a series of movements or maneuvers, like those of drilling soldiers.
A garden plant with clusters of small purple flowers and a sweet, vanilla-like scent.
A small round sweet; figuratively, flattery or praise.
To stare with an angry or sullen look.

Sir Walter Scott’s historical romance (1819), set in 12th-century England in the days of Richard the Lionheart, full of knights, tournaments and sieges. Scott’s novels were favorites of American readers.
The Wicket Gate and the Hill Difficulty
In Bunyan’s The Pilgrim’s Progress, Christian enters the narrow way through a small Wicket Gate and later has to climb a steep slope called the Hill Difficulty.
Also in Bunyan, a stately house beside the road built for the rest and refreshment of pilgrims. Two lions stand in the way near its gate and frighten travelers.

Polite families did not simply drop in on neighbors they had not been introduced to. Acquaintance usually began with a formal call by the adults, so children of different households might live side by side without ever speaking.

Neighbors showed kindness to an invalid by sending a covered dish, flowers or something to amuse them. Soft, plain foods such as jellies, custards and blancmange were thought suitable for a sore throat or a weak appetite.
Wealthy families often educated a son at home with a private tutor, usually a young college graduate, to prepare him for university.
A large house of the period might have a library with busts, cabinets of coins and curiosities, a heated conservatory, a drawing-room with a grand piano, and half a dozen servants.
A mild old oath meaning “what the devil”; it has nothing to do with Charles Dickens.
A gentleman of the old school offered a lady his arm to lead her into a room or to the table, even a young girl.

quiz.q: Why does Jo head out with a broom and a shovel?
o: To clear the walk for Mr. Laurence’s carriage
To build a snow fort with Beth and Amy
To dig paths and look for an adventure
To shovel out the cellar door for Hannah
quiz.e: She sweeps a path round the garden for Beth and the invalid dolls, then digs her way to the hedge once Mr. Laurence has driven off.

quiz.q: Why has Laurie been shut up indoors?
o: A sprained ankle
A broken arm
A fever
A bad cold
quiz.e: He croaks “as hoarsely as a raven” that he has had a bad cold and been shut up for a week.

quiz.q: What does Jo bring when she visits Laurie?
o: Amy’s drawings and Meg’s cake
Meg’s blancmange and Beth’s kittens
Hannah’s turnovers and one of Beth’s dolls
Marmee’s flowers and Jo’s own play
quiz.e: The blancmange is garlanded with leaves and Amy’s geranium flowers; laughing over the kittens makes Laurie forget his bashfulness.

quiz.q: How has Laurie come to know the March girls by sight?
o: He watches their lit window from his room
Mr. Brooke points them out on their walks
He has seen them all at church on Sundays
His grandfather described the family
quiz.e: He admits that when the curtain is left up it is “like looking at a picture,” and adds that he has no mother. Jo promises never to draw that curtain again.

quiz.q: What story makes Laurie laugh until he cries?
o: Jo’s account of the burnt hair at the party
Jo’s imitation of Aunt March shouting “Josy-phine!”
The tale of Amy’s fall into the coal-hod
Aunt March’s parrot pulling off a suitor’s wig
quiz.e: Jo tells of the prim old gentleman who came to woo Aunt March and lost his wig to Poll, the parrot that talks Spanish.

quiz.q: Not knowing he is behind her, what does Jo say about Mr. Laurence’s portrait?
o: That he looks proud and she is afraid of him
That he looks very like her own father
That he has kind eyes and she likes him
That the portrait flatters him a great deal
quiz.e: She adds that his mouth is grim and he isn’t as handsome as her grandfather; he answers “Thank you, ma’am,” and is pleased by her honesty.

quiz.q: According to Mrs. March, why might Mr. Laurence dislike hearing Laurie play?
o: It recalls the Italian musician his son married
The piano was a gift to his late wife
He finds the noise bad for his headaches
Laurie plays badly and will not practise
quiz.e: He never saw his son after that marriage; Laurie takes after his mother, and the old man may fear he will want to be a musician.

quiz.q: What does Beth hope the big house might become for them?
o: Their Celestial City
Their Palace Beautiful
Their House of the Interpreter
Their Delectable Mountains
quiz.e: Beth links it to their Pilgrim’s Progress game, and Jo replies that first “we have got to get by the lions.”

chapters.title: Beth Finds the Palace Beautiful
chapters.intro: Background on The Pilgrim’s Progress, winter pastimes, needlework gifts, the language of flowers and the parlor piano, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: A person who gives help or money to others.
To stay away from lessons or school without permission.
To treat someone too tenderly and protectively.
A convent of nuns; jokingly, any quiet household of women and girls.
Short for tableaux vivants, “living pictures”: scenes in which costumed people pose silently and motionless, like a painting.
A weakness or failing, of body or character.
Something offered to tempt or attract someone.
A short, entertaining story about a real incident or person.
A book of practice pieces for a musical instrument, or a notebook for school exercises.
Bad-tempered and easily irritated, especially of an old person.
To make lively gestures with the hands and arms while speaking.
An upright piano in a tall, cabinet-like wooden case, smaller than a grand.
An old name for the wild pansy, a small purple-and-yellow flower.
In John Bunyan’s The Pilgrim’s Progress, a stately house beside the pilgrims’ road where travelers are welcomed, fed and rested. Two lions near the gate stand in the way of anyone approaching it.
An echo of the Bible’s First Letter of John: “There is no fear in love; but perfect love casteth out fear.”
A formal, old-fashioned way of closing a letter, used between equals and even to children; it did not mean the writer was actually a servant.
In snowy New England, young people went skating on ponds and on sleigh rides, and spent evenings at charades, tableaux and small parties at one another’s houses.

Women often worked the tops of slippers in wool embroidery on canvas, a popular style called Berlin work. The finished pieces were then taken to a shoemaker to be “made up” into actual slippers, a favorite homemade gift for a gentleman.
Victorians gave flowers symbolic meanings. The pansy, whose name comes from the French pensée, “thought,” stood for thoughts and remembrance.
A piano was the center of musical life in a comfortable 19th-century home, and playing it was a prized accomplishment for girls. It was also costly, far beyond the means of a poor family.
Pianos need regular tuning and drift out of tune when left unplayed or in damp rooms; a well-cared-for instrument was tuned by a professional tuner.

quiz.q: Besides old Mr. Laurence, what is the other “lion” in the way?
o: Mr. Brooke, Laurie’s strict tutor
Being poor while Laurie is rich
Aunt March’s disapproval
Their fear of the servants
quiz.e: The girls are shy of favors they cannot return, until they see that Laurie considers them the benefactors.

quiz.q: How does Mr. Laurence respond when Laurie keeps skipping lessons?
o: He lets him go, saying the boy needs young company
He forbids the visits until his studies improve
He asks Mr. Brooke to teach the girls as well
He sends Laurie back to school in Switzerland
quiz.e: He admits he has been “coddling the fellow” and says Mrs. March is doing more for him than they can.

quiz.q: Why did Beth run away on her first visit to the big house?
o: A servant told her the piano was locked
Laurie began to play and she felt ashamed
She heard the old gentleman scolding Laurie
Mr. Laurence stared and said “Hey!” loudly
quiz.e: He frightened her so much her “feet chattered on the floor,” and she vowed never to go again, not even for the piano.

quiz.q: How does Mr. Laurence win Beth over to using his piano?
o: He sends Laurie over with a formal written invitation
He offers to pay for proper music lessons
He asks if the girls would keep his piano in use
He leaves Marmee a key to the side-door
quiz.e: Talking music until Beth creeps closer, he asks whether some of the girls would practise “just to keep it in tune,” promising nobody will see them.

quiz.q: When he kisses Beth, whom does Mr. Laurence say her eyes remind him of?
o: His late wife, long ago
A little girl he once had
Laurie’s Italian mother
His own sister as a child
quiz.e: “I had a little girl once, with eyes like these,” he says, and leaves in a great hurry.

quiz.q: What does Beth make for Mr. Laurence to thank him?
o: Slippers worked with pansies
A bookmark stitched with roses
A scarf knitted in dark purple
Handkerchiefs marked with his name
quiz.e: Pansies on a deeper purple ground; with Laurie’s help the slippers are smuggled onto his study table with a short note.

quiz.q: What does Mr. Laurence send Beth in return?
o: A set of new songs and exercise-books
A music box from his travels abroad
A little piano that was his granddaughter’s
A key to the drawing-room for her very own use
quiz.e: The cabinet-piano belonged to “the little granddaughter he lost”; his letter calls heart’s-ease his favorite flower.

quiz.q: What does Beth do that astonishes her family?
o: Plays a concert for the neighbors at once
Writes him a long letter of thanks that night
Sends Laurie to thank him on her behalf
Walks over alone and kisses him in his study
quiz.e: Forgetting her speech, she puts her arms round his neck and kisses him; Meg declares “the world is coming to an end!”

Latin for “a slip of the tongue”: saying one word when you meant another.
A schoolmaster in Charles Dickens’s Dombey and Son (1846–48) who crams his pupils with Greek and Latin with little thought for their happiness.
A proverb based on Proverbs 16:18: “Pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall.”

Children might attend a free public school or a small private school run by a single teacher. Learning meant memorizing and reciting, and Latin, Greek and arithmetic were highly prized.
Striking pupils on the palm with a ruler or rod was a common school punishment in the 19th century, though some parents and educational reformers objected to it.
Limes preserved in salt brine were shipped to New England from the Caribbean and sold cheaply by the piece. They were a popular treat among schoolchildren.
Old cloth rags could be sold to a ragman, who resold them to paper mills, since paper was then made from cotton and linen rags. Children could earn a little pocket money this way.

quiz.q: When Amy called Laurie “a perfect Cyclops,” what did she actually mean to call him?
o: A Cossack
A centaur
A cavalier
A Titan
quiz.e: Jo laughs that “that little goose means a centaur”: Amy was admiring his riding, not his eyes.

quiz.q: Why did Amy tell Meg she was “dreadfully in debt”?
o: She owed a classmate for a lost slate pencil
She had borrowed drawing paper from Jenny
She had promised her whole set a party
She owed schoolmates a dozen pickled limes
quiz.e: Limes were the school fashion and treats were “debts of honor”; Amy had accepted many and returned none, and Marmee had forbidden buying on credit.

quiz.q: Who told Mr. Davis that Amy had limes in her desk?
o: Jenny Snow
Katy Brown
Mary Kingsley
Susie Perkins
quiz.e: Jenny Snow, whom Amy had pointedly refused any limes, took her revenge, knowing the teacher had declared limes contraband.

quiz.q: What did Mr. Davis make Amy do with the limes?
o: Eat one in front of the whole class
Hand them round to the other girls
Throw them out of the window two by two
Leave them on his desk until recess
quiz.e: Amy made six trips to the window, and the Irish children in the street cheered as the limes fell.

quiz.q: According to the narrator, what finally decided Mr. Davis to strike Amy?
o: A faint hiss from one of the girls
Amy’s refusal to apologize
Jenny Snow’s laughter at Amy
The disgusting smell of the limes
quiz.e: Amy was rather a favorite, and the narrator believes he would have relented had one “irrepressible young lady” not hissed.

quiz.q: After the blows, what further punishment did Mr. Davis give Amy?
o: Writing lines until the end of the day
Staying behind after school with him
Losing her place as best map-drawer
Standing on the platform until recess
quiz.e: She stood fifteen minutes before the whole school, eyes fixed on the stove-funnel, and it felt like an hour.

quiz.q: What was Mrs. March’s view of the affair?
o: She blamed only Jenny Snow for telling tales
She disliked his methods but felt Amy earned a penalty
She thought Amy should go back the next morning
She agreed with Mr. Davis in every particular
quiz.e: Marmee disapproves of corporal punishment and takes Amy out of school, but says Amy broke the rules and is getting “rather conceited.”

quiz.q: Who was the girl Laurie described as having a remarkable musical talent she knew nothing about?
o: Jo March
Amy March
Beth March
Meg March
quiz.e: Laurie meant Beth, who turned red and hid her face in a sofa-cushion; Jo let him win at chess to repay the compliment.

A Swedish novelist (1801–1865) whose stories of family life were widely read in English translation.
Scottish author (1771–1832) of historical novels such as Waverley and Ivanhoe, hugely popular for family reading.
An Anglo-Irish writer (1768–1849) known for moral tales for children and for novels such as Castle Rackrent.
St. Paul’s letter to the Ephesians (4:26) says, “Let not the sun go down upon your wrath”: settle a quarrel before the day ends.
Jesus’s words to his disciples in the garden of Gethsemane (Matthew 26:41): “Watch and pray, that ye enter not into temptation.”
Spectacular stage shows drawn from fairy tales, with imps, elves, princesses, bright lights and scenery that changed as if by magic, were popular entertainments in the mid-1800s.
Respectable girls did not sit alone at a public entertainment; they went in a party with family or a trusted escort, and good seats could be reserved in advance.
Many families spent the evening sewing while one member read aloud, then gathered round the piano to sing hymns and songs.
Hundreds of thousands of Northern men served in the Civil War as soldiers, chaplains or hospital workers. Their wives ran the household alone, often on very little money.

quiz.q: How did Amy work out where her sisters were going?
o: She overheard Laurie talking to Hannah
She found the tickets in Jo’s pocket
She saw Meg slip a fan into her pocket
She read a note Laurie had left for Jo
quiz.e: The fan gave it away: Amy guessed at once that they were off to the theatre to see “the Seven Castles.”

quiz.q: Why did Meg say Amy could not go to the play that week?
o: Her eyes were too weak yet for the bright stage
She had not finished her lessons for the week
Mother wanted her home to keep Beth company
There was no money left for another ticket
quiz.e: Amy had been shut up with a cold, and Mother felt her eyes could not yet bear the light of the fairy piece; she could go the next week with Beth and Hannah.

quiz.q: When Jo came home from the play, what did she check first, expecting revenge?
o: Her writing desk in the garret
Her best gloves and boots
The chest of play costumes
Her bureau and its top drawer
quiz.e: In their last quarrel Amy had tipped Jo’s top drawer onto the floor; this time everything seemed in place, so Jo thought she was forgiven.

quiz.q: What had Amy done with Jo’s book of fairy tales?
o: Hidden it in the attic
Burned it in the fire
Torn out the pages
Given it to Laurie
quiz.e: Jo had just made a fair copy and destroyed the old one, so the fire consumed “the loving work of several years.”

quiz.q: What did Marmee whisper to Jo at bedtime that night?
o: “Forgive her, for she is younger than you are”
“Pride goes before a fall, my dear”
“A soft answer turneth away wrath”
“Don’t let the sun go down upon your anger”
quiz.e: She urged, “forgive each other, help each other, and begin again tomorrow,” but Jo felt too injured to forgive yet.

quiz.q: How did Jo and Laurie get Amy out of the river?
o: Laurie held her up while Jo dragged over a fence rail
Jo lay flat on the ice and pulled her out by the hood
Laurie skated for help and two men brought a ladder
Jo threw her scarf and Laurie hauled her to the bank
quiz.e: Laurie, lying flat, held Amy up “by his arm and hockey” until Jo brought a rail from the fence; Amy was “more frightened than hurt.”

quiz.q: What did Marmee confess to Jo about her own temper?
o: She had never once lost it since her marriage
She had cured it entirely as a young girl
She had struggled with it for forty years
She had only ever lost it with Aunt March
quiz.e: “I am angry nearly every day of my life,” she says; she has learned to control it, but not yet to stop feeling it.

quiz.q: What gesture did Mr. March use to help his wife check her temper?
o: He would take her hand
He put a finger to his lips
He would quietly leave the room
He tapped on the table
quiz.e: Jo had noticed him do it; Marmee says she asked him to, and his kind look saved her “from many a sharp word.”

An object thought to give protection or good luck.

Embroidery done with colored wool yarn on canvas.
An ointment or cream; a tinted salve could redden the lips.

In John Bunyan’s The Pilgrim’s Progress, a fair kept all year long in the town of Vanity, where every kind of worldly pleasure and honor is for sale. The name came to mean fashionable society and its empty show; Thackeray borrowed it for his novel Vanity Fair (1847–48).
A fable from Aesop in which a jackdaw decks itself in feathers dropped by other birds to look grand, and is stripped of them by the birds they belong to.
A girl “came out” into society in her late teens, after which she attended adult balls and dinners and could receive callers and suitors. Before that she was expected to dress and behave simply.
Fashionable ladies spent afternoons paying short formal visits to one another’s homes, often leaving printed calling cards.
A long, elaborate group dance, also called the cotillion, often closing a ball, with figures led by one couple and small favors handed out.
A middle-class woman of the 1860s had few ways to earn a living, so marriage largely decided her comfort and standing. The scheming, matchmaking mother was a stock figure of fun.
A common, often unkind name for a woman who never married.
Families on small means “turned” worn dresses inside out and retrimmed them to look new, or remade old silks in a newer style.
A lady did not go out or to a party without gloves, so a clean pair was a mark of respectability.
Ball gowns were cut low to bare the shoulders, while day dresses were high-necked. Tight lacing, long trains and high-heeled boots were the height of fashion.
Sprinkling one’s talk with French words, and employing a French maid, signaled fashion and refinement among wealthy Americans.

quiz.q: Why was Meg free to go on her visit to the Moffats?
o: The children she taught had the measles
Aunt March had gone away for the spring
Mrs. March had given her a holiday
The Kings had left for the seashore
quiz.e: Meg calls the measles “the most fortunate thing in the world,” since it freed her for a fortnight at Annie Moffat’s.

quiz.q: What did Marmee give Meg out of her treasure-box?
o: An old pearl set and a length of violet silk
A coral bracelet and a lace collar
Silk stockings, a carved fan and a blue sash
A set of silver filagree with earrings
quiz.e: Meg wanted the violet silk, but there was no time to make it over; Marmee thought real flowers prettier for a young girl than the pearls.

quiz.q: Why was Meg disappointed in her new umbrella?
o: It was too heavy and old-fashioned to carry
It was green, not black with a white handle
It had a broken rib that showed when open
It was an old one that Aunt March had cast off
quiz.e: Mother forgot and bought a green one with a yellowish handle; Meg refused to change it rather than hurt Marmee’s feelings.

quiz.q: Who sent the box of roses, heath and fern before the small party?
o: Ned Moffat
Belle’s George
Major Lincoln
Laurie
quiz.e: Annie assumed they were for Belle, but they came for Meg from Laurie, with a note from her mother.

quiz.q: What did Meg overhear while sitting just inside the conservatory?
o: That the Moffats meant her to marry their Ned
Gossip that Marmee planned a match with Laurie
That her gown was the prettiest in the room
Major Lincoln asking for her to sing again
quiz.e: “Mrs. M. has made her plans,” said Mrs. Moffat, and the voices called her dress a “dowdy tarlatan”; the gossip spoiled Meg’s easy friendship with Laurie.

quiz.q: How did Meg tease the Moffat girls about the “Mr. Laurence” they had invited?
o: She said he was nearly seventy
She said he was already engaged
She said he never went to parties
She said he was away at college
quiz.e: She pretended they meant old Mr. Laurence, then called Laurie “only a little boy,” to the sisters’ puzzled looks.

quiz.q: What did Laurie tell Meg he didn’t like about her looks that evening?
o: Rouge and powder
Frills and furbelows
Curls and lace
Fuss and feathers
quiz.e: His bluntness stung Meg, who called him “the rudest boy I ever saw,” though he soon came back to beg her pardon.

quiz.q: What did Meg overhear Major Lincoln say about her?
o: That she sang better than any girl present
That she was the prettiest girl at the party
That they had made her “nothing but a doll”
That she would make a charming bride for Ned
quiz.e: “They have spoilt her entirely,” he told his mother, which made Meg wish she had worn her own things.

quiz.q: What favor did Meg ask of Laurie while they danced?
o: Not to tell her family about her dress
To dance every waltz with her that night
To keep Ned Moffat away from her
To take her home before the supper
quiz.e: She wanted to confess to her mother herself; Laurie promised “Silence à la mort,” though he disliked seeing her drink champagne and flirt.

quiz.q: What did Marmee say she would rather see her daughters be than “queens on thrones” without self-respect?
o: Teachers or writers earning their own bread
Rich men’s wives in splendid houses
Daughters who never left their mother’s home
Poor men’s wives, if happy and beloved
quiz.e: Her “plans” are for her girls to marry for love, not money; when Jo says they’ll be old maids, then, Marmee agrees that is better than an unhappy marriage.

Charles Dickens’s first novel (1836–37). Mr. Samuel Pickwick, founder of the Pickwick Club, travels with three members and records their adventures: the romantic Tracy Tupman, the would-be poet Augustus Snodgrass, and Nathaniel Winkle, who claims sporting skills he lacks.
Mr. Pickwick’s witty, loyal Cockney servant in the same novel, famous for comic sayings and for pronouncing v as w.
An old saying meaning to seize an opportunity. Time was pictured as bald except for a lock of hair on his forehead, which had to be grabbed as he came.
In Genesis 11, people build a tower to reach heaven, and God confuses their language so they can no longer understand one another.
Francis Bacon (1561–1626), English essayist and philosopher, and John Milton (1608–1674), poet of Paradise Lost, were ranked with Shakespeare among the giants of English writing.
Fraternal orders such as the Freemasons and the Odd Fellows, with badges, rituals and private meetings, were extremely popular in 19th-century America.
Clubs copied the rules of a legislature: a president in “the Chair,” members proposing “motions,” and votes taken by calling out “Ay” or “No.”
A 19th-century label, often mocking, for women who campaigned for women’s rights and lectured in public, a daring thing for a woman then.
New Englanders baked squash or pumpkin into a pie with milk, eggs, sugar and spice, a favorite autumn dish.
Families and young friends sometimes produced their own handwritten newspapers of stories, poems, jokes and mock advertisements as a pastime.

quiz.q: What was Jo growing in her quarter of the garden this year?
o: Roses, heliotrope and a little orange-tree
Sweet peas, mignonette and larkspur
A bower of honeysuckle and morning-glories
Sunflowers, to feed her hen and chicks
quiz.e: Jo’s bed was “never alike two seasons”; the sunflower seeds were for “Aunt Cockle-top” and her chicks. Meg grew roses, Beth old-fashioned flowers, and Amy had a bower.

quiz.q: Which Pickwickian name did Amy take in the club?
o: Samuel Pickwick
Nathaniel Winkle
Augustus Snodgrass
Tracy Tupman
quiz.e: Amy, “always trying to do what she couldn’t,” was Winkle; Meg was Pickwick, Jo was Snodgrass and Beth was Tupman.

quiz.q: In “The Masked Marriage,” who was revealed beneath the bridegroom’s mask?
o: The English artist Ferdinand Devereux
Count Antonio, as everyone expected
A troubadour who loved the queen
The count’s own nephew from Venice
quiz.e: The artist lover had become the Earl of Devereux and De Vere, so the ambitious count could not refuse him.

quiz.q: What did the paper’s article “The Public Bereavement” mourn?
o: The loss of Jo’s best pen and inkstand
The death of Aunt Cockle-top, the speckled hen
The disappearance of the cat Snowball Pat Paw
The theft of Amy’s plaster casts and pencils
quiz.e: Last seen watching the butcher’s cart, Snowball was feared stolen; a mournful poem signed “A. S.” followed.

quiz.q: In the Weekly Report, which member was marked “Bad”?
o: Meg
Jo
Beth
Amy
quiz.e: The report read: Meg, Good; Jo, Bad; Beth, Very good; Amy, Middling. A hint also asked “A. S.” not to whistle in the street.

quiz.q: On the first vote, who joined Jo in saying “Ay” to admitting Laurie?
o: Meg
Amy
No one
Beth
quiz.e: Beth gave a timid Ay, then stood up to declare “he may come, and his grandpa, too, if he likes,” which carried the second vote.

quiz.q: Where had Laurie been during the club’s debate about him?
o: In the closet, sitting on a ragbag
Behind the garret curtain
Up in the old apple-tree
On the stairs outside the door
quiz.e: Jo flung open the closet door to reveal him “flushed and twinkling with suppressed laughter”; he joined as Sam Weller.

quiz.q: What did Laurie give the club in thanks for admitting him?
o: A printing press for the paper
A new lamp and set of badges
A post office in the old martin-house
A shelf of books from his grandfather’s library
quiz.e: Each “nation” had a key to the box in the hedge, and soon the old gentleman and even his gardener were using it too.

quiz.q: Why did Jo run round the corner as Aunt March’s carriage drove off?
o: She had forgotten to fetch Aunt March’s spectacles
She was late to meet Laurie down at the river
She feared being asked to go along to Plumfield
She wanted to be first home with the news
quiz.e: Jo thought Plumfield “about as gay as a churchyard” and fled before her aunt could finish asking, “Josy-phine, won’t you—?”

quiz.q: How long did Marmee allow for the “all play and no work” experiment?
o: One week
One month
Three days
The whole summer
quiz.e: She predicted that by Saturday night they would find “all play and no work is as bad as all work and no play.”

quiz.q: What went wrong with the blue muslin Meg bought?
o: The color faded badly in the summer sun
It was too narrow to make a full skirt
She left it behind in the shop by mistake
It wouldn’t wash, though she had already cut it
quiz.e: She discovered it “wouldn’t wash” only after cutting the breadths off, which made her slightly cross.

quiz.q: How did Mrs. March bring the experiment to a head on Saturday?
o: She sent the girls to stay with the Laurences
She gave Hannah a holiday and kept to her room
She hid the larder keys and went to Aunt March
She invited Miss Crocker to dine with them all
quiz.e: There was no fire, no breakfast and no mother in sight; Marmee wanted them to feel “the full effect of the play system.”

quiz.q: Why had Pip the canary died?
o: Beth had forgotten to feed him
Amy left his cage in the sun
The cat got into the parlor
Jo let the fire go out overnight
quiz.e: There wasn’t “a seed or a drop” left; Beth blamed herself, and Jo offered her domino-box for a coffin.

quiz.q: Who arrived unexpectedly and announced she had come to dinner?
o: Sallie Gardiner
Annie Moffat
Miss Crocker
Kate Vaughn
quiz.e: The gossiping spinster came just after Marmee left; the girls disliked her but were kind because she was old and poor.

quiz.q: What spoiled Jo’s strawberries and cream?
o: Unripe berries and cream that was too thin
Salt instead of sugar, and sour cream
The cat had got at the cream in the larder
Berries left too long by the hot stove
quiz.e: She had powdered the berries from the wrong box and forgotten to put the milk in the refrigerator; at Laurie’s twinkling eyes she burst out laughing.

quiz.q: What did Meg resolve to do at the end of the experiment?
o: Learn plain cooking for her holiday task
Do her lessons every day without fail
Learn to make buttonholes properly
Make the set of shirts for her father
quiz.e: Jo vowed to learn plain cooking, Beth to study, Amy to make buttonholes, and Meg to sew Father’s shirts instead of fussing over her own clothes.
