items: A postal service that carried letters cheaply, for about a penny; used loosely of anyone delivering mail.
A small bunch of flowers, often sweet-smelling.
A light cotton cloth, usually woven in checks or stripes.
A festive party or outdoor celebration.
Strips of paper around which hair was wound overnight to make curls.
A hat of fine plaited straw, named after the Italian port of Livorno (called Leghorn in English).
In rowing, to turn the oar blade flat as it moves back through the air.
In croquet, one of the small arches or hoops the balls must pass through.
The officer in charge of an army’s food and supplies.
Suffering from indigestion; by extension, gloomy or irritable.
A stiff cotton fabric with a raised, ribbed or quilted-looking weave.
A dictionary, especially one of an ancient language such as Greek.
Gloomy and hollow-sounding, like a voice from a tomb.
A lively solo dance traditionally associated with sailors.
In older use: languishing and feebly sentimental, sighing in an affected way.

A lawn game in which players knock wooden balls through a course of hoops with mallets, finishing at a stake. It became a craze in England and America in the 1860s. To “croquet” an opponent is to set your ball against theirs and strike your own, sending theirs flying.
A rigmarole is a long, rambling, disconnected story. As a parlor game, one player begins a tale and stops at an exciting moment, and the next must carry it on.
A party game in which a player chosen by lot must answer every question put by the others honestly.
A popular nineteenth-century card game in which players collect sets of cards naming famous writers and their works.
The name of a chase game and of a board game, in both of which one “fox” tries to catch the “geese.”
In John Bunyan’s The Pilgrim’s Progress, the winged fiend the pilgrim Christian must fight. Readers used the name for any besetting fault or enemy.
Maria Stuart (1800), a verse tragedy by the German poet Friedrich Schiller about the last days of Mary, Queen of Scots, who was executed in 1587.
To respectable English and American readers of the time, French novels suggested racy, overwrought romance.
A stout, blunt cartoon figure who stands for England or the English, as Uncle Sam stands for the United States.
The patriotic fervor of the American Revolution, named after 1776, the year of the Declaration of Independence.
Respectable young unmarried women were expected to have an older woman present at mixed gatherings, to “play propriety.”
In England a governess was often a gentleman’s daughter without money, teaching in a wealthy household. Her position was awkward: neither servant nor family.
A wide riding track in London’s Hyde Park, where fashionable people rode and were seen; often called simply “the Row.”

quiz.q: What is odd about the mail Meg receives from the little post office?
o: Her letter is in Laurie’s handwriting
Her posy for Marmee was taken by mistake
Only one of her pair of gloves is there
Her German song is still untranslated
quiz.e: Meg left a pair of gray cotton gloves at the Laurences’ but only one came back. She thinks Mr. Brooke translated her song.

quiz.q: What does Laurie send Jo, partly as a joke?
o: An old broad-brimmed hat
A box of chocolate drops
A plaster bust of Plato
A picture to copy
quiz.e: Jo had said she wished bigger hats were in fashion, so Laurie sent an old Leghorn “to try me.” She wears it to the picnic.

quiz.q: Why does Marmee’s letter make Jo’s eyes fill with tears?
o: It says Father will be home by autumn
It forgives her for the quarrel with Amy
It asks her to look after Beth at the picnic
It praises her efforts to control her temper
quiz.e: Jo thought no one saw her struggles. She pins the note inside her frock “as a shield and a reminder.”

quiz.q: What does Fred Vaughn do during the croquet game?
o: Hides Jo’s ball among the nettles
Nudges his ball through with his toe
Moves the stake while no one is looking
Knocks Kate’s ball out of the game
quiz.e: His ball stopped on the wrong side of the wicket, and he gave it “a sly nudge with his toe.” Jo saw him and called it cheating.

quiz.q: How does Jo win the croquet game?
o: She croquets Fred’s ball into the bushes
Fred is put out of the game for cheating
She spares Kate’s ball and makes a clever stroke
Laurie gives up his own turn so she can play
quiz.e: “Yankees have a trick of being generous to their enemies,” Jo says, leaving Kate’s ball untouched before winning.

quiz.q: Who begins the story in the game of Rigmarole?
o: Kate, with a count rescuing a lady
Mr. Brooke, with a poor knight
Ned, with a scholar and his lexicon
Fred, with a warship and pirates
quiz.e: Kate asks Mr. Brooke to begin; his knight tames a king’s colt and looks for a face he has seen in dreams. The others each carry the tale on.

quiz.q: In the game of Truth, what does Jo finally admit she most wishes for?
o: Genius
Fame
A horse
Courage
quiz.e: She first says “a pair of boot-lacings,” but is made to answer truly: “Genius; don’t you wish you could give it to me, Laurie?”

quiz.q: How does Kate react when Meg says she is a governess herself?
o: She offers to find Meg a post in England
She asks Meg to teach Grace some German
She praises American girls’ independence
She treats Meg with plain condescension
quiz.e: Her “Oh, indeed!” implied “Dear me, how dreadful!” It is Mr. Brooke who says American girls are respected for supporting themselves.

quiz.q: What does Mr. Brooke tell Meg he will do once Laurie goes to college?
o: Take a tutoring post abroad
Become a soldier, as he is needed
Go back to college to study law
Find work in Mr. Laurence’s firm
quiz.e: “As soon as he is off, I shall turn soldier. I am needed.” He adds, rather bitterly, that few people would care whether he lived or died.

quiz.q: What subject finally gets Frank Vaughn talking happily with Beth?
o: Cricket
Boating
Buffaloes
Fox-hunting
quiz.e: After her blunder about hunting, Beth turns to the prairies, which she knew from one of Jo’s boys’ books. Grace says she hasn’t heard Frank laugh so much in ages.

chapters.title: Castles in the Air
chapters.intro: Background on The Pilgrim’s Progress and other references, the overseas trade of New England merchants, and nineteenth-century dreams of art and music abroad, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: A large shade tree with broad, many-fingered leaves and shiny brown nuts.
A flat case for carrying loose drawings or papers.
In knitting a sock, to work the shaped part that fits around the heel.
A fixed amount of work given to someone to do.
To waste time; to move or act slowly and idly.
In a sulky, peevish, bad-tempered way.
Deserving respect because of great age; often used jokingly to mean simply “old.”
Contrary to one’s natural inclination, like planing wood the wrong way.
The state of being under someone else’s control.
A passing feeling of hurt pride or irritation.
Of tea, to steep in hot water until the flavor comes out.
A child’s first reading book, often full of moral lessons.

John Bunyan’s allegory (1678) of the pilgrim Christian’s journey from the City of Destruction to the Celestial City, meaning heaven. Traditional pilgrims carried a staff and a scrip, a small bag for provisions.

In Bunyan’s book, pleasant mountains where shepherds let the pilgrims glimpse the gate of the Celestial City far off. Before entering the city, pilgrims must cross a deep river, and shining angels come to welcome them.
An old phrase for daydreams and grand plans that may never come true.
Isaac Watts’s much-taught children’s hymn begins “How doth the little busy bee / Improve each shining hour,” praising industry over idleness.
In the Bible, young David played the harp to soothe the troubled King Saul, so a musician who calms a gloomy listener might be called a “little David.”
Merchants in New England ports grew rich from ships trading with India and China, bringing home tea, silk and spices. Sons were often expected to take over the family business.
During the Civil War, women and girls at home knitted socks, mittens and scarves for Union soldiers, often through local soldiers’ aid societies.
In the nineteenth century, Germany was the great center of musical training, and ambitious American musicians went to study at conservatories such as Leipzig’s.
Rome drew painters and sculptors from all over Europe and America, who came to study ancient and Renaissance art and to work in its studios.

quiz.q: What sort of day has Laurie had before he spots the March girls?
o: A busy day of lessons and errands
An idle, cross and unsatisfactory one
A happy day out riding with his tutor
A tiring afternoon at the gymnasium
quiz.e: He shirked his studies, tried Mr. Brooke’s patience, frightened the maids and quarreled with the stableman before flinging himself into his hammock.

quiz.q: What is peculiar about the girls’ appearance as they set out?
o: They carry a picnic hamper and fishing rods
They wear their best dresses and bonnets
They carry sketchbooks and folding stools
They have big hats, pouches and long staffs
quiz.e: Each wears a flapping hat, carries a brown linen pouch and a long staff, as they play pilgrims while they work.

quiz.q: What do the sisters call the hill where they work?
o: The Delectable Mountain
The Celestial City
The Hill Difficulty
The Valley of Humiliation
quiz.e: From it they can look far away and “see the country where we hope to live some time,” as the pilgrims do in Bunyan.

quiz.q: What is Meg’s favorite castle in the air?
o: A life of music and travel in Germany
Fame as a great painter in Rome
A lovely house full of luxuries
A stable of horses and rooms of books
quiz.e: She wants nice food, pretty clothes, servants and “heaps of money,” though she would “do good, and make everyone love me dearly.”

quiz.q: What is Beth’s wish?
o: To have a little piano of her own
To fly away to the Celestial City
To become a famous musician
To stay safe at home with the family
quiz.e: She already has her piano and wants only that they “may all keep well and be together.”

quiz.q: How old does Meg say she will be when they meet again in ten years?
o: Twenty-seven
Twenty-six
Twenty-four
Twenty-two
quiz.e: Meg has just turned seventeen. Jo works out the rest: she and Laurie will be twenty-six, Beth twenty-four and Amy twenty-two.

quiz.q: What does Mr. Laurence want Laurie to become?
o: A college professor
An India merchant
A concert pianist
An army officer
quiz.e: Laurie hates “tea and silk and spices” and says he would rather be shot, but there is no one else to stay with the old gentleman.

quiz.q: What does Laurie decide that night while Beth plays for his grandfather?
o: To run away to sea on one of the ships
To study music in Germany after college
To let his dream go and stay with him
To ask Mr. Brooke to remain his tutor
quiz.e: Watching the old man grieve for his dead child, Laurie resolves: “I’ll let my castle go, and stay with the dear old gentleman while he needs me.”

chapters.title: Secrets
chapters.intro: Background on newspapers and women writers, Shakespeare and Greek myth, and town life in the 1860s, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: An attic room just under the roof of a house.
A tin reflector oven, set in front of an open fire to roast meat.
A library that lent books to members for a fee.
A large horse-drawn passenger vehicle running along a fixed route.
A public room for a particular activity, such as billiards.
The sport of fighting with blunted swords.
A light round box for hats or collars; someone shut up in one is kept away from the world.
To fake someone’s signature or a document in order to deceive.
Someone who gets their way by flattery and coaxing.
Choice and desirable, like a plum picked out of a pudding.
Untidy, with hair and clothes in disorder.
French for “as it should be”: correct and proper in manners.
An exaggerated piece of praise or advertisement in a newspaper.
To wet with drops, as with dew or tears.
Weekly newspapers of the period filled many columns with sensational and romantic fiction, much of it by unknown or anonymous writers.
Writing for papers and magazines was one of the few respectable ways a nineteenth-century woman could earn money at home.
Fanny Burney’s novel Evelina (1778), published anonymously when she was a young woman, made her famous once her authorship became known.
Shakespeare’s Hamlet ends with a fencing match between Hamlet and Laertes, a favorite scene for amateur actors.
In Greek myth, a swift huntress who would marry only a man who could beat her in a footrace. One suitor won by dropping golden apples that she stopped to pick up.
An eagle shown with wings and legs outstretched, an emblem on American coins and seals, and so a symbol of national pride.
Pulling a bad tooth was the usual cure. Ether anesthesia had been demonstrated in Boston in 1846, but a visit to the dentist was still widely dreaded.
Billiards at home was a gentleman’s pastime, but public billiard rooms were linked in many minds with gambling, drinking and idle young men.
After the Great Famine of the 1840s, many poor Irish families settled in and around New England’s cities.

quiz.q: Where does Jo keep her papers safe from Scrabble the rat?
o: In an old tin kitchen on the wall
In a locked trunk beneath the old sofa
In a hatbox beneath the eaves
In Marmee’s writing desk
quiz.e: Scrabble, “of a literary turn,” liked to make a circulating library of any book left out by eating the leaves.

quiz.q: How does Jo slip out of the house without being seen?
o: Through the little gate at the back
By the kitchen door while Hannah naps
Out a window and down a porch roof
Over the fence into Laurie’s garden
quiz.e: She got out of the back entry window onto the roof of a low porch, swung down to the bank and took a roundabout way to the road.

quiz.q: When Jo comes down the stairs, what does Laurie think she has been doing?
o: Taking a lesson in fencing
Having teeth out at the dentist
Calling on the editor of a newspaper
Buying a present for Meg
quiz.e: A dentist’s sign hung at the entrance, so he asks, “How many did you have out?” Jo laughs: there are two she wants to have “come out” in a week.

quiz.q: What was Laurie doing in the building opposite?
o: Playing billiards with Ned Moffat
Visiting a newspaper office
Sitting for his portrait
Taking a lesson in fencing
quiz.e: Jo accuses him of being in a billiard saloon, but it was a gymnasium. He admits he does sometimes play billiards in town with Ned and his set.

quiz.q: What is Jo’s secret?
o: She has had two teeth pulled
She has left two stories with a newspaper
She is writing a play for Laurie
She has entered a writing prize
quiz.e: The newspaper man is to give his answer next week. Laurie hails “Miss March, the celebrated American authoress.”

quiz.q: What is Laurie’s secret about?
o: A letter for Jo from Father
Who translated Meg’s song
Belle Moffat’s coming wedding
Where Meg’s missing glove is
quiz.e: He whispers three words: it has been in someone’s pocket “all this time.” Jo is disgusted “at the idea of anybody coming to take Meg away.”

quiz.q: Why is Jo glad that Meg envies Belle Moffat’s wealth?
o: She thinks Meg deserves a fine life
She means to buy Meg some silk dresses
She hopes Meg won’t marry a poor man
She wants Meg to see Paris one day
quiz.e: “If you care much about riches, you will never go and marry a poor man,” Jo says, while Laurie silently warns her to be careful.

quiz.q: What did the newspaper pay Jo for her stories?
o: Nothing, since it never paid beginners
A dollar each, paid on publication
Five dollars for the pair of them
A year’s free copies of the paper
quiz.e: The editor printed and “noticed” them as good practice. Laurie means to get the next one paid for, and Jo dreams of supporting herself.

chapters.title: A Telegram
chapters.intro: Background on the Civil War home front, wartime Washington, and money and medicine in the 1860s, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: A wheel turned by people or animals walking on it; by extension, dull, endless routine.
A system for sending messages along wires by electrical signals; also used for a message sent this way.
A task or errand someone carries out on another person’s behalf.
Rubber overshoes worn over ordinary shoes in wet weather.
Acting hastily, without thinking of the consequences.
An old name for a small coin; to grudge a ninepence is to grudge a trifling sum.
Joking slang for one’s own hair.
During the Civil War the Union capital filled with military hospitals, many set up in hotels, churches and public buildings, to treat sick and wounded soldiers.

Women volunteered as nurses in Union hospitals, many under Dorothea Dix, the Superintendent of Army Nurses. Louisa May Alcott nursed in a Washington-area hospital in 1862–63 until she fell ill herself.
Telegrams were charged by the word, so messages were kept short and blunt. Most families sent and received them only rarely, for urgent matters.
A Union private was paid about thirteen dollars a month for most of the war, which gives a sense of what a few dollars meant to an ordinary family.
From 1862 the Union government issued paper money, nicknamed “greenbacks,” to help pay for the war.
By the 1860s railroads linked New England with Washington by way of New York, Philadelphia and Baltimore, though the trip meant changes of train and long hours of travel.

quiz.q: What is Meg complaining about at the start of the chapter?
o: That Jo always has ink on her nose
That the Kings work her far too hard
That Father’s letters keep coming late
That nothing pleasant ever happens
quiz.e: Out of sorts, she says they “go grubbing along day after day” and that it is “a dreadfully unjust world.”

quiz.q: What does the telegram say?
o: Mr. March is wounded; come quickly
Mr. March is very ill; come at once
Mr. March is coming home on leave
Mr. March has been taken prisoner
quiz.e: “Your husband is very ill. Come at once.” It is signed S. Hale, from a hospital in Washington.

quiz.q: Who is the first to stop crying and set the household working?
o: Meg
Mrs. March
Hannah
Laurie
quiz.e: Hannah wipes her face on her apron, says she won’t waste time crying, and goes off “to work like three women in one.”

quiz.q: Who offers to escort Mrs. March to Washington?
o: Mr. Brooke
Mr. Laurence
Laurie
Dr. Bangs
quiz.e: Mrs. March would not let old Mr. Laurence make the journey, so he gives Mr. Brooke commissions in Washington and sends him instead.

quiz.q: What does Mrs. March do with Aunt March’s reply?
o: Sends the money back with a polite note
Reads the scolding note aloud to the girls
Burns the note and keeps the money
Passes the note on to Mr. Laurence
quiz.e: The note said it had been absurd for March to join the army. Mrs. March put it in the fire and the money in her purse, lips folded tightly.

quiz.q: How much money does Jo bring home for her father?
o: Twenty-five dollars
Forty dollars
Thirty-five dollars
Fifty dollars
quiz.e: She sold her hair to a barber. Forty dollars was the price marked on a black tail of hair in his window.

quiz.q: Who persuades the barber to buy Jo’s hair?
o: Laurie, who happened to be passing
A customer who admired its color
The barber’s young apprentice
The barber’s wife, with a son in the army
quiz.e: The barber said it wasn’t a fashionable color, but his wife said, “Take it, Thomas,” thinking of her son Jimmy, a soldier.

quiz.q: Why is Jo crying in bed that night?
o: She fears Father will die
She grieves for her lost hair
She misses Marmee already
She regrets a quarrel with Meg
quiz.e: “My—my hair!” She insists she is not sorry and would do it again; it is only “the vain, selfish part” of her crying.

chapters.title: Letters
chapters.intro: Background on The Pilgrim’s Progress and an old Scottish song, Civil War places and army terms, and washday and letter-writing at home, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: A long towel sewn into a loop and hung on a wooden roller, usually in the kitchen.
A small pie made by folding pastry over a filling.
Here, an ornamental figure of a Chinese official with a head that nods when touched.
An official message or report, especially one sent from a war zone.
A fine, dependable person who can be relied on.
A dove known for its soft cooing, long a symbol of gentle affection.
A thick pad of cloth for handling hot pots and pans.
To confirm or support what someone else has said.
A powder mixed with water to stiffen washed linen and clothes.
A blue dye added to the rinse water to make white laundry look whiter.
A cheap, often printed cotton cloth.
Thinking ahead; getting things done in good time.
A soldier, or small group, posted ahead of a camp to keep watch for the enemy.
In the second part of Bunyan’s The Pilgrim’s Progress, Great-heart is the strong, kind guide who escorts and protects the pilgrim Christiana and her children on their journey.
A gentle Scottish song by Lady Nairne. “Leal” means loyal or faithful, and “the land o’ the leal” is heaven, where the faithful go after death.
A river in Virginia where Union and Confederate armies faced each other for long stretches of the war; the Battle of Fredericksburg was fought on its banks in December 1862.
The army officer responsible for quarters, clothing and supplies, as the commissary is for food.
A formal parade of troops in full uniform, held for inspection or on a special occasion.
Monday was traditionally washing day. Clothes were soaked, scrubbed and boiled, then rinsed, blued, starched, wrung and hung out to dry: a long, heavy day’s work.
Paper and postage cost money, so letters were often written on thin, lightweight sheets and filled to the edges; a scented sheet was a small luxury.

quiz.q: What motto does Marmee leave her daughters as she departs?
o: Pray and be patient
Be brave and be good
Hope and keep busy
Work hard and wait
quiz.e: “Hope and keep busy; and whatever happens, remember that you never can be fatherless.” The girls adopt it as their motto.

quiz.q: What name do the girls give Mr. Brooke as he sets off with their mother?
o: Mr. Greatheart
Sir Knight
Colonel Teddy
Mr. Valiant-for-truth
quiz.e: He looked “so strong and sensible and kind” that they christened him after the guide in The Pilgrim’s Progress.

quiz.q: What makes the girls break down in tears once their mother has gone?
o: Her empty chair at the breakfast table
Father’s last letter lying on the desk
Her old gown hanging in the closet
The stockings she mended for them
quiz.e: Beth points to the pile of nicely mended hose on Mother’s table, proof that she thought of them even in her last hurried moments.

quiz.q: How does Hannah bring the girls round after their crying?
o: With fresh hot turnovers
With a pot of coffee
With a chapter of the Bible
With a walk in the garden
quiz.e: Coffee was a treat, and in ten minutes they were “all right again.” Hannah later reports she lets them have it only once a week.

quiz.q: What does Jo’s letter tell Marmee about her and Laurie?
o: They quarreled and made up at the gate
They rowed up to Longmeadow for a picnic
They started a newspaper for Father
They argued with Aunt March over Amy
quiz.e: Remembering Marmee’s words when Amy fell into the river, Jo ran over to apologize and met Laurie at the gate coming to do the same.

quiz.q: What is Amy’s complaint about Laurie in her letter?
o: He won’t take her out driving
He laughs at her clay models
He calls her Chick and talks French
He spelled her name wrongly
quiz.e: He talks French to her very fast when she says “Merci” or “Bon jour,” which hurts her feelings now that she is “almost in my teens.”

quiz.q: What washing mishap of Jo’s does Hannah report?
o: She scorched Meg’s best collar
She starched clothes before rinsing
She let the clean wash blow into the mud
She boiled Amy’s woolen stockings
quiz.e: Jo starched the clothes before they were “wrenched” and blued a pink calico dress, which nearly made Hannah die laughing.

quiz.q: What does Mr. Laurence offer in his short letter to Mrs. March?
o: To come to Washington himself
To send Laurie down to help her
To find Mr. March a better doctor
To pay any expenses beyond her estimate
quiz.e: “Draw on me for funds if expenses exceed your estimate. Don’t let your husband want anything.”

chapters.title: Little Faithful
chapters.intro: Background on childhood illness and home medicine, charity visiting, and immigrant families in the 1860s, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: This chapter includes the death of a young child and a serious infectious illness.
So gradually as to be hardly noticed.
A homeopathic remedy made from arsenic diluted many, many times.
A falling back into a former state, such as an old habit or an illness.
The swinging weight that keeps a clock running and regular.
Saying or doing things that don’t agree with each other.
A portion or dish of cooked food.
A strong-smelling substance from a tree, used in medicines and to keep moths away.
Deadly nightshade, a poisonous plant; tiny doses were used as medicine.
Coaxing and flattering, in order to persuade.
Going about from place to place in search of fun.
A light carriage pulled by a fast-trotting horse.
Staying power; the strength to keep going or to resist illness.
Powdered tobacco, sniffed up the nose a pinch at a time.

A contagious infection, most common in children, that brings a sore throat, high fever and a bright red rash. Before antibiotics it was a much-feared and often deadly disease, and people believed one attack protected against another.

A system of medicine founded by the German doctor Samuel Hahnemann around 1800, using extremely diluted doses of substances. It was very popular in nineteenth-century America, and many families kept a homeopathic medicine chest and guidebook at home.
Middle-class women and girls often visited poor families in their neighborhood, bringing food, clothing, firewood and help with the children.
Large numbers of Germans came to the United States in the 1840s and 1850s. Many arrived poor and worked long hours in the cities.
Parrots were fashionable pets, prized for repeating phrases they had overheard, often at the worst possible moment.

quiz.q: What happens to the girls’ good resolutions once their first worry about Father eases?
o: They grow stricter with themselves
They slowly slip back into old ways
They write to Marmee twice a day
They take on all of Hannah’s chores
quiz.e: They felt that “Endeavor deserved a holiday, and gave it a good many.” Only Beth keeps faithfully to her little duties.

quiz.q: Why is Jo kept at home instead of going to Aunt March’s?
o: Aunt March has gone visiting friends
She is finishing a story for the paper
Meg needs her help with the sewing
She has caught a bad cold in the head
quiz.e: She caught cold by not covering her shorn head enough, and Aunt March didn’t like to hear people read with colds.

quiz.q: Which poor family has Beth been visiting every day?
o: The Hummels
The Kings
The Gardiners
The Mullets
quiz.e: Mother told them not to forget the Hummels, but Meg and Jo each put off going, so Beth went alone again.

quiz.q: What happens while Beth is holding the Hummel baby?
o: It starts to recover
Its fever breaks at last
It dies in her lap
It falls fast asleep
quiz.e: It gave a little cry, trembled and lay still before Mrs. Hummel came back with the doctor.

quiz.q: What illness does the doctor find in the Hummel children?
o: Measles
Diphtheria
Whooping cough
Scarlet fever
quiz.e: Heinrich and Minna have sore throats. The doctor tells Beth to go home and take belladonna at once, or she will have the fever.

quiz.q: Whom does Beth choose to stay home and nurse her?
o: Meg
Jo
Hannah
Amy
quiz.e: Meg offers as the oldest and Jo because she feels it is her fault, but Beth says “Jo, please,” which settles it.

quiz.q: How does Laurie persuade Amy to go to Aunt March’s?
o: By promising daily visits and outings
By offering her a new box of paints
By saying Aunt March would be hurt
By telling her Beth asked her to go
quiz.e: He promises to come every single day, take her out with Puck, go to the theater and fetch her home the minute Beth is well.

quiz.q: How does Laurie make Amy laugh instead of cry at Aunt March’s?
o: By making faces behind Aunt March
By mimicking the old lady’s voice
By slyly pulling the parrot’s tail
By hiding the old lady’s spectacles
quiz.e: Polly croaks “Bless my boots!” and later mimics Aunt March, but once they leave, the parrot’s rudeness makes Amy sniff after all.

chapters.title: Dark Days
chapters.intro: Background on nineteenth-century illness and home nursing, the telegraph and wartime travel, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: This chapter includes serious illness in a child.
A bedspread; the top cover laid over a bed.
A return of an illness after a person had seemed to be getting better.
A cloth or garment in which a dead person is wrapped for burial.
Someone looked after, protected or helped by another person. From French, “protected one.”
Comfort in a time of sadness or distress.
The innermost feelings. To “warm the cockles of your heart” is to give deep, glowing pleasure.
Through someone else acting in your place.
In an old kitchen, a sideboard or set of shelves for dishes, with a flat top that could be sat on.
A state of near-unconsciousness, in which a person hardly responds to anything.
A group of cannon and the soldiers who fire them.
Pale and weak-looking, as from illness or tiredness.
Another word for a burial shroud; used figuratively of anything that covers like a pale sheet.
A period of staying awake through the night to watch over someone or to pray.

A contagious infection, most common in children, that causes a high fever, a very sore and swollen throat and a red rash. Before antibiotics it was widely feared, because it could be dangerous or leave lasting damage, and healthy children were often sent away to avoid catching it.
A very high fever can bring on delirium: confusion, rambling speech, and failing to recognize familiar people or places.

Nineteenth-century doctors and nurses often spoke of a fever “turning” or reaching its “crisis”: a point at which the patient would either begin to recover or grow worse. Families waited anxiously for it.

Most sick people in the 1860s were cared for at home rather than in hospital. A doctor made house calls, but the daily nursing fell to family members and servants, who sat up through the night in turns.
In the nineteenth century a small glass of wine was commonly given as a pick-me-up to someone faint, exhausted or in shock.

By the 1860s telegraph wires linked American towns and cities. A message was handed in at a telegraph office, sent in Morse code, and delivered at the other end by messenger within hours, where a letter took days. Telegrams were charged by the word, so they were short and usually meant urgent news.

During the Civil War, Washington, D.C., was crowded with army camps and military hospitals. Disease killed more soldiers than battle did, and relatives sometimes traveled there to nurse the sick and wounded.
Railroads ran passenger trains through the night, so a traveler from a distant city might arrive at a small-town station in the small hours. Winter storms could delay them badly.

quiz.q: Why did Meg feel guilty when writing her letters home in the first days of Beth’s illness?
o: She had quarreled with Jo over who should nurse Beth
She left out Beth’s illness, as Hannah insisted she must
She had spent the money meant for Beth’s medicine
She had stayed away with the Kings instead of helping
quiz.e: Meg had been told to mind Hannah, and Hannah “wouldn’t hear of Mrs. March bein’ told, and worried just for sech a trifle.”

quiz.q: What news in a letter from Washington added to the sisters’ trouble?
o: Mr. Brooke had fallen ill with fever
Mrs. March had been delayed by snow
Mr. March had been moved to Baltimore
Mr. March had suffered a relapse
quiz.e: Mr. March had had a relapse and “could not think of coming home for a long while.”

quiz.q: Who came to the house to beg pardon for her thoughtlessness and to get a shroud for Minna?
o: Mrs. Hummel
Aunt March
Mrs. Moffat
Mrs. King
quiz.e: Poor Mrs. Hummel came, one of the many neighbors and tradespeople who showed how many friends shy Beth had made.

quiz.q: What did Dr. Bangs say to Hannah on the morning of the first of December?
o: Beth must be moved to the Laurences’ house
Jo must stop nursing Beth for a while
Mrs. March had better be sent for
Beth would be out of danger by night
quiz.e: He said, “If Mrs. March can leave her husband, she’d better be sent for,” and Jo ran out into the storm with the telegram.

quiz.q: When Laurie asks whether Meg does her fair share, what does Jo call Beth?
o: My conscience
My comfort
My good angel
My right hand
quiz.e: “Beth is my conscience, and I can’t give her up. I can’t! I can’t!” Jo cried, breaking down for the first time.

quiz.q: What secret did Laurie reveal to cheer Jo up?
o: He had brought a second doctor to see Beth
He had written to Amy at Aunt March’s house
He had found a nurse to help Hannah at night
He had telegraphed Mrs. March the day before
quiz.e: Brooke had answered that she would come at once; Laurie planned to meet the two a.m. train.

quiz.q: Why had Laurie sent the telegram in spite of Hannah?
o: Dr. Bangs had privately asked him to send it
He and his grandfather felt Mrs. March ought to know
Meg had begged him to send it without telling Hannah
Jo had written the message and asked him to take it
quiz.e: He and Mr. Laurence thought Hannah was “overdoing the authority business,” and Laurie could never bear to be “lorded over.”

quiz.q: What did Meg do with the white rose that bloomed in the night?
o: Laid it in Beth’s hand while she slept
Sent it over to Mr. Laurence with a note
Set it where Beth would see it on waking
Pinned it to her dress to greet Mother
quiz.e: She put it in her vase so that the first things Beth saw on waking would be “the little rose, and mother’s face.”

A will (formally a “last will and testament”) says who is to receive a person’s property after death. It is signed by the person making it and, to be valid, by witnesses who watch the signing.

Important papers were once folded and sealed with sealing wax, melted at a small candle called a taper and pressed with a stamp. Legal documents were often tied with red ribbon, which is where the phrase “red tape” comes from.
Latin for “in the year of the Lord.” Formal documents sometimes gave the date this way, and A.D. is its abbreviation.
Nineteenth-century New England was overwhelmingly Protestant. Catholics were mostly immigrants, from Ireland above all, and also from France and French Canada, and they often met with suspicion.

Catholics use the beads of a rosary to count the prayers of a set devotion, such as repeated Hail Marys. Most Protestants of the time did not use beads and regarded the practice as foreign to their own worship.
Paintings of Mary holding the infant Jesus, by artists such as the Italian Renaissance master Raphael, are among the most famous in the world. Engraved or painted copies hung in many homes.
A “Testament” is a New Testament printed on its own. A small Testament and a hymnbook were common possessions of a Protestant child.
Nineteenth-century mourners wore black jewelry such as jet, and treasured lockets or brooches holding a lock of a loved one’s hair, sometimes woven into tiny pictures such as weeping willows.
A young woman “came out” when she was formally introduced into adult society, after which she went to balls and could be courted.
Old trunks and wardrobes often held clothes from earlier fashions: stiff brocade gowns, quilted petticoats, high-heeled shoes and turbans, which were fashionable for women in the early 1800s.
The great Gothic cathedral of Paris, a favorite subject for prints and for drawing students to copy.

quiz.q: Apart from Laurie, who made Amy’s stay at Aunt March’s bearable?
o: Hannah, on her visits
The deaf old coachman
Esther, the French maid
Kitty Bryant, her friend
quiz.e: Esther was “the only one who ever took any notice of the young lady,” amusing her with stories of France and letting her explore the house.

quiz.q: On what condition had Esther agreed to change her name from Estelle?
o: That she never be asked to change her religion
That she be allowed to visit France each year
That she be named in her mistress’s will
That she be given charge of the jewel-cases
quiz.e: Aunt March ordered the change, and she obeyed on condition that she was never asked to change her religion: she was a devout Catholic.

quiz.q: What did Esther suggest to help Amy in her loneliness?
o: Writing a letter to Beth every evening
Wearing the gold-and-ebony rosary
Reading from her French prayer book
Going apart each day to pray quietly
quiz.e: Esther advised her to go apart each day “to meditate and pray,” and fitted up a little dressing-room as a chapel.

quiz.q: According to Esther, who would receive Aunt March’s pearls?
o: Whichever niece nursed Beth through her illness
Whichever niece was the first to be engaged
Whichever niece behaved best that winter
Whichever niece came to live with her
quiz.e: “The first one who is affianced will have the pearls,” Esther whispered; she fancied the turquoise ring would go to Amy.

quiz.q: What hung above the table in Amy’s little chapel?
o: A portrait of Aunt March as a young belle
An engraving of Notre Dame cathedral
A sketch of Beth that Amy had drawn
A fine copy of a famous Madonna painting
quiz.e: Esther borrowed it from a shut-up room thinking it of little value, but it was a valuable copy of “one of the famous pictures of the world.”

quiz.q: Why did Amy hang up the rosary Esther gave her instead of using it?
o: She doubted it suited Protestant prayers
She feared Aunt March would scold her
She thought it too fine for daily use
She had lent it to Laurie for a joke
quiz.e: She felt “doubtful as to its fitness for Protestant prayers,” though she used the chapel every day.

quiz.q: Why did Amy leave Jo her most precious plaster rabbit?
o: To thank Jo for nursing Beth so faithfully
To replace an inkstand cover Jo had lost
To make amends for burning up Jo’s story
To keep a promise she made at Christmas
quiz.e: The will says she leaves it “because I am sorry I burnt up her story.”

quiz.q: After hearing how Beth had given away her things, what codicil did Amy add?
o: That her turquoise ring go to Beth
That her curls be cut and given to friends
That Esther keep her clay horse and her fan
That Laurie choose any sketch he likes
quiz.e: Laurie smiled at “Amy’s last and greatest sacrifice”: all her curls cut off and given round to her friends, though it would spoil her looks.

chapters.title: Confidential

A person who hoards money and loves it for its own sake.
Friendly, pleasant and easy to talk to.

Crossing in different directions; muddled or tangled.
In respectable nineteenth-century families a young man was expected to speak to a girl’s parents, usually her father, before courting her seriously or proposing marriage.
A man was expected to be able to support a wife before marrying, so couples of modest means often waited years while he saved money or became established in a profession or business.
Outside the family, adults usually addressed each other by title and surname, such as “Mr. Smith.” Calling a man by his first name implied close friendship or a family-like intimacy.
Wealthy families often hired a tutor, usually an educated young man of small means, to prepare a son for college. It was respectable work but poorly paid.
A young man without family money needed a steady position, such as a clerkship or a share in a business, before he could keep a household free of debt.
During the Civil War the sick and wounded in Washington’s hospitals were often nursed with help from volunteers and visiting relatives, alongside army surgeons.

In the Gospel of Matthew, Jesus tells his followers to pray in private: “enter into thy closet, and when thou hast shut thy door, pray.” Many devout Protestants kept a quiet corner for prayer and reading.
Christian art often shows Jesus as a baby on his mother Mary’s knee, a reminder that he was once a small child.

quiz.q: When Beth first woke from her long, healing sleep, what did she see?
o: Her father’s letter and Laurie
Her cats and Jo asleep in a chair
Hannah and Dr. Bangs at the door
The little rose and her mother’s face
quiz.e: Meg’s tender hope was realized: the first objects Beth saw were “the little rose and mother’s face.”

quiz.q: What did Laurie do at Aunt March’s while Amy wrote a note to her mother?
o: He read the newspaper aloud to Aunt March
He fell sound asleep on the sofa
He taught Polly a new phrase
He rode off to meet the next train
quiz.e: Amy saw he was dropping with sleep and persuaded him to rest; Aunt March pulled down the curtains in “an unusual fit of benignity.”

quiz.q: What did Amy say she wanted the turquoise ring to remind her of?
o: To be patient with her aunt
To keep her temper with Jo
To cure herself of selfishness
To pray every day for her sisters
quiz.e: Selfishness was the largest of her “bundle of naughties,” and she meant to try to be like Beth.

quiz.q: According to Jo, what had first given away Mr. Brooke’s feelings for Meg?
o: He kept one of Meg’s lost gloves
He wrote verses about her in his notebook
He sang her favorite song at the Laurences’
He asked Laurie which flowers she liked
quiz.e: One of the gloves Meg left at the Laurences’ fell out of his waistcoat pocket, and when Laurie teased him he owned that he liked Meg.

quiz.q: What had John Brooke told Mr. and Mrs. March about Meg?
o: That he meant to propose to her at Christmas
That he would earn a comfortable home before proposing
That he hoped to take her back to Washington
That he would ask Mr. Laurence to speak for him
quiz.e: He loved her but would earn a comfortable home before asking her to marry him; he wanted only leave to love her and work for her.

quiz.q: Before what age had Mr. and Mrs. March agreed Meg should not bind herself or marry?
o: Eighteen
Nineteen
Twenty
Twenty-one
quiz.e: Meg was only seventeen; her parents agreed she should not be engaged or married before twenty, so the love could be tested by waiting.

quiz.q: Whom had Jo privately planned for Meg to marry?
o: Laurie
Ned Moffat
Fred Vaughn
Frank Vaughn
quiz.e: Jo wanted Meg to marry Teddy and “sit in the lap of luxury,” but her mother thought him too young and “too much of a weathercock.”

quiz.q: How did Meg answer when her mother said she called Mr. Brooke “John”?
o: That it sounded far too familiar
That she would rather not talk about him
That Father might think it improper
That she was glad, as he was so lonely
quiz.e: Meg’s quiet answer led Mrs. March to conclude, “She does not love John yet, but will soon learn to.”

chapters.title: Laurie Makes Mischief, and Jo Makes Peace

To win over or calm someone who is displeased, by doing something to please them.

The Life of Samuel Johnson (1791) by James Boswell, a long, lively biography of the English writer and dictionary-maker, full of his conversation and sayings. It was a standard book in gentlemen’s libraries.
A short philosophical tale (1759) by Samuel Johnson about a prince of Abyssinia who leaves his sheltered valley to search for the secret of happiness.
A series of moral essays that Samuel Johnson wrote and published twice a week in the early 1750s.
In Homer’s Odyssey, Mentor is the old friend left in charge of Odysseus’s son, and the goddess Athena takes his form to give the boy advice. His name came to mean a wise adviser.

From Charles Dickens’s novel Little Dorrit, in which a starchy governess advises saying “papa, potatoes, poultry, prunes and prism” to give the lips a pretty shape. The phrase became shorthand for prim, ladylike propriety.
The heroine of Maria Edgeworth’s novel Patronage (1814), admired as a model of good sense and prudence.
From the nursery rhyme Humpty Dumpty: after his fall, “all the king’s horses and all the king’s men” could not put him together again.
A gentleman of the period was expected to keep a promise once given, even under pressure; breaking one’s word was a serious mark against one’s character.
Among gentlemen, a serious insult could once lead to a challenge and even a duel. A formal written apology, worded with great ceremony, was the accepted way to settle such a quarrel honorably.

quiz.q: What did Laurie manage to find out after pestering Jo about her secret?
o: That it concerned Meg and Mr. Brooke
That it concerned Amy and her new ring
That it concerned Jo’s newest story
That it concerned Mr. March’s health
quiz.e: He wheedled, bribed and threatened until he was satisfied the secret was about Meg and his tutor, and felt slighted that Brooke had not confided in him.

quiz.q: How was the love letter Meg received signed?
o: “Your faithful Brooke”
“Your loving Theodore”
“Your devoted John”
“Your humble tutor”
quiz.e: The note, written “in a peculiar hand,” begged Meg to send “one word of hope through Laurie to Your devoted John.”

quiz.q: What had Meg written in reply to the first note?
o: That she loved him and would wait for him
That she was too young, and he must ask Father
That she could never care for him at all
That she would answer once Mother was home
quiz.e: She said she was too young, didn’t want secrets from her mother, and would be his friend, “but nothing more, for a long while.”

quiz.q: What did Jo decide after studying both notes closely?
o: That Ned Moffat had written the first
That Mr. Brooke wrote only the second
That Amy had copied Mr. Brooke’s hand
That Laurie had written both of them
quiz.e: Jo declared that Brooke never saw either letter: “Teddy wrote both, and keeps yours to crow over me with.”

quiz.q: Why had Mr. Laurence shaken Laurie?
o: Laurie had been rude to the housemaid
Laurie had skipped his lessons for days
Laurie would not tell what had happened
Laurie had spent his money on a journey
quiz.e: Laurie had promised not to tell, and when his grandfather “collared” him for the truth he bolted upstairs and locked himself in.

quiz.q: What wild plan did Laurie propose to Jo?
o: To sail for India on a merchant ship
To run off to Washington and surprise everyone
To join the army as drummer boys
To ride to Boston and stay with friends
quiz.e: Jo would surprise her father and Laurie would “stir up old Brooke.” She was tempted but refused: as a girl, she “must be proper, and stop at home.”

quiz.q: Why did Mr. Laurence’s face change when Jo warned that Laurie might run away?
o: Laurie had once run off to sea for a week
Mr. Laurence had run away himself as a boy
Laurie’s tutor had threatened to leave him
Laurie’s father had run away in his youth
quiz.e: He glanced at the portrait of Laurie’s father, who “had run away in his youth, and married against the imperious old man’s will.”

quiz.q: What did Jo find in Meg’s desk while hunting for stamps?
o: A paper scribbled with “Mrs. John Brooke”
A pressed flower from Mr. Brooke’s bouquet
A second letter signed by Mr. Brooke
A sketch of Mr. Brooke that Amy drew
quiz.e: Jo threw it in the fire, feeling that Laurie’s prank had “hastened the evil day”: Meg never mentioned Brooke but thought of him a good deal.

In older usage, a dish or portion of soft food, especially for a sick person.

Impossible to carry out in practice.

John Bunyan’s Christian allegory (1678). In Part One a man named Christian journeys from the City of Destruction to the Celestial City, joined along the way by companions called Faithful and later Hopeful, and passing through trials and places of rest.
In Part Two of Pilgrim’s Progress, travelers in the Valley of Humiliation hear a shepherd boy singing a song about humility and contentment that begins, “He that is down needs fear no fall.”

Two romances by the German writer Friedrich de la Motte Fouqué, popular in English translation. Undine (1811) tells of a water spirit who gains a soul by marrying a mortal knight; Sintram and His Companions (1815) follows a troubled young knight’s struggle against evil.
Raphael (1483–1520) was an Italian Renaissance painter, famous above all for his gentle pictures of the Madonna and Child.
A popular nickname for Queen Elizabeth I of England.
An echo of the old English carol “God Rest You Merry, Gentlemen,” which says “let nothing you dismay.”
Famous snowy peaks of the Alps. Jungfrau, in Switzerland, means “maiden” in German; Mont Blanc, on the border of France and Italy, is the highest mountain in the Alps.
The Puritan founders of New England had frowned on celebrating Christmas, but by the mid-1800s it had become a cheerful family holiday with gifts, carols and a large dinner.
People of the period often had locks of family members’ hair, living or dead, woven or set into brooches, rings and lockets as tokens of affection.

quiz.q: How did Amy celebrate her return home?
o: By sketching each of her sisters in turn
By giving away as many treasures as she could
By reading aloud to Beth every afternoon
By cooking delicate dishes for the invalid
quiz.e: “A loyal slave of the ring,” she gave away as many of her treasures as her sisters would accept. It was Meg who cooked for Beth.

quiz.q: What Christmas surprise did Jo and Laurie make for Beth?
o: A snow-maiden crowned with holly
A sleigh trimmed with red ribbon
A bonfire with a string of skyrockets
A triumphal arch over the gate
quiz.e: “The Unquenchables” built a snow-maiden in the garden, bearing gifts and a carol on a pink streamer, “The Jungfrau to Beth.”

quiz.q: What Christmas gift did Meg receive?
o: A pair of fine kid gloves, from Aunt March
A gold bracelet, from her father
A string of pearls, from Mr. Laurence
Her first silk dress, from Mr. Laurence
quiz.e: Meg smoothed “the silvery folds of her first silk dress; for Mr. Laurence had insisted on giving it.”

quiz.q: On whose arm was Mr. March leaning when he arrived?
o: Mr. Laurence’s
Laurie’s
Mr. Brooke’s
Dr. Bangs’s
quiz.e: Laurie announced “another Christmas present,” and a tall man appeared, “leaning on the arm of another tall man”: Mr. Brooke.

quiz.q: In the joyful confusion, what did Mr. Brooke do “entirely by mistake”?
o: He tumbled over a stool
He nearly fainted away
He sobbed over the turkey
He kissed Meg
quiz.e: Amy tumbled over a stool, Jo nearly fainted, Hannah sobbed over the turkey, and Mr. Brooke kissed Meg “entirely by mistake, as he somewhat incoherently explained.”

quiz.q: What did Jo mutter after seeing the look between her parents?
o: “I hate estimable young men with brown eyes!”
“I wish flatirons would keep us small!”
“Why weren’t we all born boys, then?”
“That man will make a hole in the family!”
quiz.e: Mr. March had praised Brooke as “a most estimable and upright young man,” then glanced at Meg and raised his eyebrows at his wife.

quiz.q: What did Mr. March read in Meg’s roughened hand?
o: That she had grown careless of her looks
That she had made vanity a burnt offering
That she had worked too hard for her health
That she had been sewing for the soldiers
quiz.e: “A burnt-offering has been made of vanity,” he said, valuing her homemaking skill more than “white hands or fashionable accomplishments.”

quiz.q: What did Beth sing at the little piano that evening?
o: The carol on the snow-maiden’s paper streamer
An old hymn her mother had sung to her as a baby
The shepherd boy’s song from Pilgrim’s Progress
The song Mr. Brooke had once given to Meg
quiz.e: Having read about Christian and Hopeful resting in a pleasant green meadow, she sang the shepherd boy’s song, to music she had made for her father.

Changing suddenly and unpredictably, on a whim.
A garden flower with large, often deep pink or red blooms.

An early kind of shower, in which a tank overhead released a sudden drenching of cold water.

Little Women was first published in 1868. Its success led Louisa May Alcott to write a second part, published the following year.

quiz.q: What did Laurie do when he saw Meg at the window?

Held up a valentine for her to read
Knelt in the snow like a pleading lover
Sang a love song under the window
quiz.e: He fell on one knee in the snow, beat his breast and clasped his hands; Jo said he was showing how “your John will go on by and by.”

quiz.q: What speech had Meg planned in case Mr. Brooke spoke to her?
o: That she would answer him once Father was well
That she could never marry a man without money
That he must first ask Aunt March’s leave
That she agreed with Father she was too young
quiz.e: She meant to say, “I agree with father that I am too young to enter into any engagement at present,” and walk out of the room with dignity.

quiz.q: What reason did Mr. Brooke first give for calling?
o: To fetch his umbrella
To bring Laurie’s lessons
To deliver a letter for Meg
To return a book to Jo
quiz.e: “I came to get my umbrella—that is, to see how your father finds himself today,” he said, getting confused.

quiz.q: Why did Meg suddenly tell Mr. Brooke, “I don’t choose. Please go away”?
o: She heard Jo laughing behind the door
His confident smile nettled her pride
She remembered Aunt March’s warnings
She feared her father would be angry
quiz.e: His eyes were merry and he looked sure of success; Annie Moffat’s lessons in coquetry came to mind, and “the love of power” woke in her.

quiz.q: What did Aunt March threaten if Meg married Mr. Brooke?
o: Meg would never get a penny of her money
She would forbid Amy to visit her again
She would have Mr. Laurence dismiss him
She would leave the turquoise ring to Jo
quiz.e: “If you do, not one penny of my money ever goes to you.” Ordered not to like John, Meg promptly decided that she would.

quiz.q: What did Aunt March suspect was the secret of Mr. Brooke’s liking for Meg?
o: He wanted a place in a good firm
He hoped to win Mr. March’s favor
He knew she had rich relations
He wished to stay near Laurie
quiz.e: Meg was indignant: “John is above such meanness,” she cried, defending him so warmly that Brooke, overhearing, knew she cared.

quiz.q: What did Jo cry when she burst in on her parents?
o: “Meg has sent him away, just as we planned it!”
“Aunt March has spoiled everything for all of us!”
“Laurie has played another wicked trick on Meg!”
“John Brooke is acting dreadfully, and Meg likes it!”
quiz.e: She had come down expecting to laugh over a rejected lover and found Meg on his knee instead.

quiz.q: How did Laurie console Jo about losing Meg?
o: That Meg would soon tire of Mr. Brooke
That she only went halves with Brooke
That Meg would live next door to them all
That Jo would soon have a sweetheart too
quiz.e: “You don’t give her up. You only go halves,” he said, and promised to stand by her “all the days of my life.”

quiz.q: After the war, what work did John Brooke take up to earn a home for Meg?
o: He became a bookkeeper
He became a schoolmaster
He became a bank clerk
He became a law clerk
quiz.e: He refused Mr. Laurence’s more generous offers, preferring to begin with “an honestly-earned salary” rather than borrowed money.

quiz.q: Why did Jo never go back to Aunt March?
o: Aunt March took offense at Jo’s stories
Jo was needed at home to nurse Beth
Amy took her place for drawing lessons
Jo found work at the Spread Eagle office
quiz.e: The old lady took a fancy to Amy and bribed her with drawing lessons from one of the best teachers, so Amy gave Aunt March her mornings.

quiz.q: How much did the Spread Eagle pay Jo for her “rubbish”?
o: Fifty cents a story
A dollar a column
Five dollars a story
Two dollars a column
quiz.e: At a dollar a column Jo felt herself “a woman of means,” while her real ambitions piled up as manuscript in the old tin kitchen in the garret.

quiz.q: Who named Meg’s little brown house the “Dovecote”?
o: Jo
Mr. March
Amy
Laurie
quiz.e: Laurie christened it, saying the lovers “went on together like a pair of turtledoves, with first a bill and then a coo.”

quiz.q: What was the family joke about Meg’s well-stocked linen closet?
o: Hannah had sewn and marked every piece herself
Mr. Laurence had it sent secretly through Hannah
Aunt March paid for it under Mrs. Carrol’s name
Sallie Moffat sent it to outshine Meg’s other gifts
quiz.e: Having vowed Meg wouldn’t get a cent if she married “that Brooke,” Aunt March had Mrs. Carrol buy the linen and send it as her own present. The secret leaked out.

quiz.q: What was in the knobby parcel Laurie brought “for Mrs. John Brooke”?
o: A watchman’s rattle
A brass dinner-bell
A toy savings-bank
A steam wash-boiler
quiz.e: He said it was useful in case of fire or thieves: Meg could swing it out of the window to rouse the neighborhood.

quiz.q: On the walk home, Jo says she will leave Laurie in peace if he will only do what?
o: Stop lending money to Henshaw
Give up his seventeen waistcoats
Stop teasing Amy about Parker
Let his cropped hair grow again
quiz.e: Jo objected to being seen with someone who looked “like a young prizefighter”; Laurie had cut his curls to fashionable stubble.

quiz.q: What does Laurie predict as they part at the gate?
o: That Amy will marry little Parker
That Jo will be the next to marry
That Meg will soon tire of housework
That his grandfather will refuse him
quiz.e: Jo insisted she would be the family’s old maid, but Laurie whistled and warned, “Mark my words, Jo, you’ll go next.”

quiz.q: What did Meg wear in her hair on her wedding day?
o: Orange-flowers
Blush-roses
A lace veil
Lilies of the valley
quiz.e: She refused silk, lace and orange-flowers, wearing only the lilies of the valley that “her John” liked best.

quiz.q: On arriving, what scandalized Aunt March?
o: Jo upsetting the wedding cake
The bride running out to greet her
Laurie towering over all the guests
Finding no wine on the table
quiz.e: “You oughtn’t to be seen till the last minute, child,” she said; Meg replied that she was not a show and would have her wedding as she liked.

quiz.q: What did Meg do the moment she was married?
o: Gave the first kiss to Marmee
Threw her bouquet to her sisters
Ran to hug Aunt March
Kissed her father’s hand
quiz.e: “The first kiss for Marmee!” she cried, which wasn’t “at all the thing,” the narrator admits.

quiz.q: Why was there no wine at the wedding lunch?
o: Aunt March had refused to send any wine
Jo had broken the bottles by accident
Mr. March sent it to the Soldiers’ Home
Mr. Laurence’s gift had come too late
quiz.e: Mr. March kept a little for Beth and sent the rest away, believing wine should be used only in illness.

quiz.q: What did Meg ask Laurie to do at the lunch?
o: To lead Aunt March in to lunch
To promise to give up wine
To make a toast to the bride
To look after Beth for her
quiz.e: He answered, “I promise, Mrs. Brooke!” and Jo toasted his resolution with lemonade. The narrator says the pledge was loyally kept.

quiz.q: Whose idea was it for the married guests to dance in a ring around the bride and groom?
o: Jo’s
Mr. March’s
Sallie Moffat’s
Laurie’s
quiz.e: Laurie proposed it “as the Germans do,” with the bachelors and spinsters prancing in couples outside the ring.

quiz.q: What was the “crowning joke” of the dance on the lawn?
o: Aunt March hopping off with her cane
Hannah dancing in her grand headdress
Mr. March dancing with Sallie Moffat
Mr. Laurence whirling Hannah about
quiz.e: When Mr. Laurence chasséed up to her, Aunt March tucked her cane under her arm and hopped briskly away to join hands with the rest.

quiz.q: How did Meg travel to her new home?
o: In Mr. Laurence’s carriage
By train, on a short wedding trip
On foot, on John’s arm
In a hired carriage with Jo
quiz.e: The little house was near, so her only bridal journey was the quiet walk with John from the old home to the new.

quiz.q: What brought Amy’s plaster-casting phase to an end?
o: A cast of Laurie fell on Hannah
Her own foot got stuck in plaster
Parents kept their children away
Jo smashed the casts while dusting
quiz.e: The plaster hardened around her foot, and Jo, laughing too hard as she dug her out, cut it and left “a lasting memorial.”

quiz.q: Why did Mrs. March agree to Amy’s costly plan for her drawing class?
o: She hoped the girls would help Amy’s art
Mr. Laurence offered to pay for it all
She wanted Jo to learn some manners
She let Amy learn from experience
quiz.e: Mrs. March “knew that experience was an excellent teacher” and left her children to learn alone when they would not take advice.

quiz.q: Why did nobody come on Monday?
o: Amy had written the wrong day on the cards
The beach-wagon broke down on the way
A shower at eleven kept them away
The girls had gone to another party
quiz.e: A smart shower at eleven “evidently quenched the enthusiasm” of the guests due at twelve, and the family ate the perishable food at two.

quiz.q: Why did Amy have to go into town herself on Tuesday morning?
o: To buy a lobster for the salad
To fetch the borrowed silver
To hire a bigger carriage
To buy more ice for the cream
quiz.e: Mr. March could get no lobsters, and the kittens had eaten the chicken, so Amy went to town rather than trust Jo to bring one home without paper.

quiz.q: Whom did Amy meet on the omnibus coming home?
o: Little Parker
Ned Moffat
Mr. Laurence
Mr. Tudor
quiz.e: Tudor was one of Laurie’s most elegant college friends, and Amy hoped he would get out before she did.

quiz.q: How did Amy recover when the lobster spilled out of her basket?
o: She claimed it was the old lady’s
She joked about the salad it would make
She hid the basket under her veil
She asked Tudor not to tell Laurie
quiz.e: She asked if he didn’t wish he could eat the salad and see the “charming young ladies,” which the narrator calls tact.

quiz.q: Who came back with Amy in the big carriage on Tuesday?
o: Six of her classmates
Mr. Tudor and his sisters
Only Miss Eliott
Miss Eliott and May Chester
quiz.e: Miss Eliott was the one guest who kept her promise; Jo rushed off to clear half the lunch from the table.

quiz.q: What birthday gift did Laurie later give Amy?
o: A coral lobster charm
A silver salt-spoon
A box of chocolates
A new sketchbook
quiz.e: The tiny coral lobster was for her watch-guard, and the word “fête” always produced a general smile afterward.

Giovanni Belzoni, an Italian strongman turned explorer, dug up and carried off Egyptian antiquities in the early 1800s and found the way into one of the great pyramids at Giza.

By whether her door was locked
By the position of her cap
By the ink on her black pinafore
quiz.e: Pulled low meant hard work, askew meant excitement, and thrown on the floor meant despair; nobody spoke to her until the red bow stood “gayly erect.”

quiz.q: Why was Jo at the lecture on the Pyramids?
o: She was escorting Miss Crocker
Her father had asked her to go
She wanted ideas for her novel
Laurie had given her tickets
quiz.e: She was “prevailed upon” to escort Miss Crocker, and in return for her virtue was rewarded with a new idea.

quiz.q: What did the boy beside her at the lecture tell Jo?
o: That the paper wanted new writers
That he wrote stories for the paper
That Mrs. Northbury was his aunt
That the author made a good living
quiz.e: He said Mrs. S. L. A. N. G. Northbury “makes a good living out of such stories,” which made Jo look at the page more respectfully.

quiz.q: What was Mr. March’s advice after praising the prize story?
o: Write for the Spread Eagle instead
Aim at the highest, never mind money
Save the money for your own education
Never write another such story
quiz.e: “You can do better than this, Jo. Aim at the highest, and never mind the money,” he said in his unworldly way.

quiz.q: What did Jo do with her hundred-dollar prize?
o: Sent Beth and Marmee to the seaside
Bought a new carpet for the parlor
Paid the butcher’s and grocer’s bills
Saved it to print her own novel
quiz.e: Beth came home much better, though not as plump as hoped. Later stories paid the butcher’s bill and bought the carpet.

quiz.q: What made Jo decide to publish her novel “soon”?
o: Mr. Allen’s offer of three hundred dollars
Her mother’s wish for outside criticism
Beth’s wish to see it printed soon
Amy’s advice to write a popular book
quiz.e: The unconscious emphasis Beth put on “soon,” and her wistful look, chilled Jo’s heart with “a foreboding fear.”

quiz.q: How did Jo go about cutting down her novel?
o: She cut only what Mr. Allen marked
She tried to follow everyone’s advice
She left out all of the metaphysical parts
She cut the tragedy and kept the fun
quiz.e: Like the old man and his donkey in the fable, she took everyone’s advice and suited nobody: out went description and fun, and in went more tragedy.

quiz.q: What “joke” did Jo find in the reviews of her book?
o: Critics praised parts Meg disliked
Every critic called it dangerous
It sold better than her stories
Real-life scenes were called absurd
quiz.e: The parts taken straight from life were called impossible, while those she made up were praised as “charmingly natural, tender, and true.”

quiz.q: Whom did John bring home to dinner without warning?

Jack Scott
Mr. Tudor
Laurie
quiz.e: He met his friend Scott on the way and, remembering Meg’s promise that he could bring anyone home, didn’t think to send word.

quiz.q: What plain meal did John ask for, which Meg scorned as vulgar for company?

Beef and vegetables
Cold meat, bread and cheese
Toast and warm coffee
quiz.e: He added, as a joke, “we won’t ask for jelly,” and that one hint at her failure sealed his fate.

quiz.q: How did Meg and John make peace that evening?
o: Meg kissed him on the forehead
John brought her bought jelly
John apologized as he came in
Marmee came over to make peace
quiz.e: Remembering her mother’s advice to be the first to ask pardon, Meg crossed the room and kissed him; John at once said, “Forgive me, dear.”

quiz.q: That autumn, whose company led Meg into extravagance?
o: Amy’s
Aunt March’s
Sallie Moffat’s
Florence Carrol’s
quiz.e: Seeing Sallie’s pretty things and not wanting to be pitied, Meg began buying trifles so Sallie wouldn’t think she had to economize.

quiz.q: What purchase lay heaviest on Meg’s conscience?

A rosebud bonnet
A gold watch-chain
A violet silk
quiz.e: The silk cost fifty dollars, half of it from the household fund, and it was not yet made up or trimmed.

That she was tired of being poor
That he never let her buy anything
That Sallie pitied her for marrying him
quiz.e: John answered only, “I was afraid of this; I do my best, Meg,” which hurt her more than scolding would have.

She returned the silk to the shop
She sold the silk to Amy
She sewed John a coat herself
quiz.e: Sallie bought it as a favor; Meg then ordered home the greatcoat and asked John how he liked her “new silk gown.”

Amy
Mr. Laurence
Laurie

She blushed and thanked her warmly
She said Amy had illustrated it
quiz.e: “Sorry you could find nothing better to read,” she said, then changed the subject; she saw her mistake at once and hurried away.

quiz.q: Why did Jo keep away from Mr. Tudor?
o: He had laughed at Amy’s lobster
He puts on airs and snubs his sisters
He was rude to Laurie at college
He mocked her stories in public
quiz.e: She said he “worries his father, and doesn’t speak respectfully of his mother,” and Laurie called him fast.

quiz.q: To whom had Jo bowed and smiled in the politest way, to Amy’s dismay?
o: Tommy Chamberlain
Young Mr. Lamb
Mr. Tudor
Ned Moffat
quiz.e: Tommy’s father kept a grocery store, but Jo thought him “a gentleman in spite of the brown-paper parcels.”

quiz.q: Which remark of Jo’s at Aunt March’s made Aunt Carrol cough “Ahem!”?
o: That she would rather stay home
That she cannot bear French
That favors make her feel a slave
That she means to be a reformer
quiz.e: Aunt March answered with a nod, “I told you so.” The narrator says this speech cost Jo several years of pleasure.

quiz.q: What did Aunt March say to Mrs. Carrol as the girls left?
o: That Jo must learn to hold her tongue
That she would speak to Mr. March
That Amy should help at the fair
That she would supply the money
quiz.e: “You’d better do it, Mary; I’ll supply the money,” she said, and Aunt Carrol agreed, “if her father and mother consent.”

chapters.title: Consequences
chapters.intro: Background on charity fairs, Bible sayings about kindness and some literary references, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: With hands on hips and elbows sticking out. “Elbows akimbo” suggests someone prickly or ready for a fight.
A feeling of irritation or resentment from hurt pride.
Decorating handwritten text with colored letters, borders and gold, in the style of medieval manuscripts; also a page decorated this way.
Doing what is convenient or useful rather than what is strictly fair.
A reddish-brown ink or paint, originally made from cuttlefish ink.
A current of cold air in a room (American spelling: draft).
A small room leading into a larger one.
Fine parchment made from calfskin, used for special books and documents.
French for “all together, as a group.”
Generosity of spirit, especially toward someone who has wronged you.
Meant to make peace or soothe bad feeling.
A tightly packed body of soldiers; loosely, any close group advancing together.
Delicate ornamental work of fine twisted wire, or anything made to look like it.
The mantelpiece: the shelf and frame around a fireplace.

Fairs and bazaars run by women were a favorite way to raise money for churches, the poor and other causes. During the Civil War, huge “Sanitary Fairs” raised money for the care of sick and wounded soldiers.
At such fairs, each lady or group of young ladies “took a table”: they gathered goods, arranged a stall and sold the items for the cause. The most prominent tables carried social prestige.

Middle-class women made decorative objects to sell or give: painted vases and fans, wax flowers, shell work, needlework and hand-lettered texts. Skill at such work was admired as a mark of refinement.
Victorians revived the medieval art of illumination as a hobby, copying Bible verses or mottoes onto good paper or vellum and decorating them with color and gold.
A commandment from the Old Testament (Leviticus) that Jesus names as one of the two greatest commandments in the Gospels.
From Proverbs, quoted by Saint Paul in Romans: by repaying an enemy with kindness you “heap coals of fire on his head,” making him ashamed of his hostility.
Do as you would be done by
The Golden Rule, from Jesus’s teaching: treat others as you would want them to treat you.
An old proverb: the satisfaction of doing right is reward enough, even if no one praises you.
From Walter Scott’s long poem Marmion (1808): the dying hero’s last cry to his men in battle, “Charge, Chester, charge! On, Stanley, on!” It was widely known and often quoted in fun.
A generous rich lady in George Farquhar’s comedy The Beaux’ Stratagem (1707). Her name came to mean any wealthy woman who plays the benefactor, sometimes with a hint of showiness.
The ancient Roman Forum, the ruined center of public life in old Rome. Digging there for relics of antiquity fascinated 19th-century visitors.

quiz.q: Besides Amy’s success at parties and with her art, what rumor chiefly fed May Chester’s grudge against her?
o: That the Marches had mocked her at the Lambs’
That Amy had copied the designs of her own vases
That Amy had snubbed Tudor at a late party
That Jo had put the Chesters into a story
quiz.e: Some gossip told May that the March girls had made fun of her at the Lambs’. The real culprit was Jo, whose imitation had been “too lifelike to escape detection.”

quiz.q: What did Mrs. Chester offer Amy in place of the art-table?
o: The refreshment table
The flower-table
The fancy-goods table
The children’s toy table
quiz.e: She suggested the flower-table, which the little girls had undertaken but given up on; May added that it was attractive “especially to gentlemen.”

quiz.q: When May said Amy could put her own things on her own table, what did Amy do?
o: Left them on the table and walked out
Asked Mrs. Chester to pay her for them
Gave them to the little girls to sell
Swept them into her apron and left
quiz.e: Amy took May’s kindly meant offer as a further insult and carried her work off “pell-mell” in her apron.

quiz.q: What made Amy decide, the next morning, to give her work back to May?
o: A talk with Marmee before breakfast
A note of apology left by May
A verse in her own illuminated book
Seeing May crying behind her vases
quiz.e: Turning the pages of her illuminated book, she came on “Thou shalt love thy neighbor as thyself” and thought, “I ought, but I don’t.”

quiz.q: How did the girl who had been making lemonade explain Amy’s generosity?
o: Amy only wanted to be thanked
Amy knew they wouldn’t sell at her table
Amy had been told to by her mother
Amy hoped to get the art-table back
quiz.e: “Very lovely; for she knew she wouldn’t sell them at her own table.” For a minute Amy felt that virtue was not always its own reward.

quiz.q: Who sent “a wilderness of flowers” up to Amy’s table that evening?
o: Hayes, the Laurences’ gardener
Hannah, from the Marches’ yard
Aunt Carrol’s coachman and maid
Mrs. Chester, by way of apology
quiz.e: Laurie had told Hayes to give Jo the best from their gardens; at Jo’s request Hayes sent flowers and a basket arranged “in his best manner.”

quiz.q: What did Amy whisper to Laurie to buy, as a final heaping of coals of fire?
o: Her own illuminated book
The art-table’s wax flowers
May’s unsold vases
The painted fans
quiz.e: Laurie bought May’s great vases and carried one under each arm; later they stood on the Marches’ chimneypiece as “the reward of merit for a magnanimous March.”

quiz.q: Why did Aunt Carrol invite Amy rather than Jo to go abroad?
o: Jo was needed at home to look after Beth
Jo was thought too old to suit as company
Amy was the better French scholar of the two
Jo’s own remarks about favors and French
quiz.e: Aunt Carrol quoted Jo’s own words: since “favors burden her” and she “hates French,” she would invite the more docile Amy as a companion for Flo.

chapters.title: Our Foreign Correspondent
chapters.intro: Background on Victorian London, Paris under Napoleon III, the Rhine and Heidelberg, and some songs and entertainments, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: A large house and estate in the country belonging to a wealthy family.
A coal mine together with its buildings and machinery.
A loose sleeveless cloak worn by women over a dress.
A two-wheeled horse-drawn cab for two passengers, with the driver seated high up behind.
A widow who holds a title or property from her late husband; loosely, any dignified elderly lady.
Comic slang for a footman in livery, from a character in William Makepeace Thackeray’s humorous writings.
Pale purple gloves of kid leather, worn by fashionable men.
In art, a full-size preparatory drawing for a painting or tapestry.
A four-wheeled open carriage with a folding hood.
A rider who sits on one of the horses pulling a carriage, to guide them.
A household’s silver or gold tableware.
Dashing but disreputable in look or manner.
A post-office department that holds letters until travelers call for them (French, “mail remaining”).
A very large cask for wine or beer.

Hyde Park is a great royal park in west London. Rotten Row, a sandy track along its south side, was where fashionable society rode and showed itself; the name is popularly said to come from “route du roi,” the king’s road.
The great Gothic church where English monarchs are crowned and many kings, poets and statesmen are buried.
Hampton Court and the Kensington Museum

Hampton Court is a Tudor royal palace beside the Thames, open to visitors. The South Kensington Museum, founded in the 1850s and later renamed the Victoria and Albert Museum, displayed art and design.
A British humorous weekly magazine founded in 1841, famous for its cartoons of English society.
Nephew of Napoleon Bonaparte, he ruled France as emperor from 1852 to 1870. His Spanish-born wife was the Empress Eugénie, and their only son, the Prince Imperial, was born in 1856.
The Louvre, a former royal palace, holds one of the world’s great art collections. The Tuileries Gardens stretch beside it along the Seine; the long Rue de Rivoli runs past both.
The largest cemetery in Paris, opened in 1804 and known for its elaborate tombs, many built like small chapels.
A former palace in central Paris whose arcades held fashionable shops, jewelers and cafés.

A steamboat trip up the Rhine, past castles, vineyards and cliffs, was a highlight of the European tour. Coblenz (Koblenz) sits where the Moselle meets the Rhine, opposite the great fortress of Ehrenbreitstein.
Baden-Baden and the Nassau baths were fashionable resorts where visitors took the waters, strolled and, especially at Baden-Baden, gambled at the casino.

In Greek myth, a princess of Crete who helped the hero Theseus escape the Labyrinth, was abandoned by him on the island of Naxos, and was then loved by the god Dionysus. Dannecker’s marble statue of her riding a panther was a famous sight in Frankfurt.

A huge ruined castle above the Neckar river. Its cellar holds the Great Tun, an enormous wine barrel, and its gardens were laid out by the Elector Frederick V for his English wife, Elizabeth, daughter of King James I.
A popular Irish song about a beauty living by the Lakes of Killarney, whose glance is said to be fatal to any man who meets it.
Charles Fechter, an actor celebrated on the London stage in the 1860s, especially for his Hamlet.

quiz.q: Who sang “Kate Kearney” to Amy at Queenstown, and later had a bouquet waiting in her room?
o: Fred Vaughn
Mr. Ward
Mr. Lennox
Frank Vaughn
quiz.e: Robert Lennox left the ship at Queenstown, but had his friend Ward order a bouquet with “Robert Lennox’s compliments” on the card.

quiz.q: On the train, what did the gray place Amy took for Kenilworth turn out to be?
o: A brewery
A colliery
A workhouse
A cotton mill
quiz.e: Uncle calmly answered, “No, my dear, not unless you want beer; that’s a brewery.” Flo’s “gallows” was a colliery and Amy’s lambs were geese.

quiz.q: What went wrong when Amy and Flo took a hansom cab on their own?
o: The horse went lame in Regent Street
The driver took them to the wrong park
They had no money to pay the fare
They couldn’t make the driver slow down
quiz.e: The driver sat up behind, out of reach; when Amy finally found the little door in the roof, he slowed to a funeral pace, then raced off again.

quiz.q: Who called on the travelers in London, having learned from Laurie where they would be?
o: Kate and Grace Vaughn
Fred and Frank Vaughn
Mr. Lennox and Mr. Ward
Ned and Sallie Moffat
quiz.e: Laurie’s English friends from Camp Laurence came to tea; Fred sent his “respectful compliments to the big hat,” meaning Jo.

quiz.q: Why was Fred so welcome when he turned up in Paris?
o: He knew the city’s galleries well
He had a carriage and fine horses
He had friends at the emperor’s court
He spoke French like a native
quiz.e: Uncle knew barely ten words of French and aunt’s was old-fashioned, so Fred did the “parley vooing,” as uncle called it.

quiz.q: When Fred showed Amy the flower he had kept from the Coblentz serenade, what did she tell him?
o: That Flo had thrown it, not she
That it had come from her hat
That he ought to give it back
That it was already half dead
quiz.e: Her laughing answer seemed to disgust him; he tossed the flower out of the window, and Amy wrote, “I’m afraid I’m going to have trouble with that boy.”

quiz.q: What did Amy tell her mother she meant to do if Fred asked her to marry him?
o: Refuse him until she had seen Rome
Accept, though not madly in love
Wait for her father’s permission
Put him off until he was older
