quiz.e: She liked him, he was rich and kind, and “one of us must marry well,” she reasoned; she would accept him though not madly in love.

quiz.q: Why did Fred leave Heidelberg so suddenly?
o: His father had ordered him to London
He had lost money at Baden-Baden
His brother Frank was very ill
He had quarreled with Amy’s uncle
quiz.e: A letter begged him to come home because Frank was very ill. As he said goodbye he asked, “I shall soon come back; you won’t forget me, Amy?”

chapters.title: Tender Troubles
chapters.intro: Background on courtship customs, work for educated young women, and some poets, songs and sports, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: A state of worry or uneasiness.
A guess made without firm evidence.
A weathervane shaped like a rooster; figuratively, a person who changes their mind easily.
A daydream, or a state of being lost in pleasant thought.
Moody, brooding and romantically gloomy, like the heroes of Lord Byron’s poems.
A tin reflector oven that stood before an open fire to roast meat.
A collection of animals kept for show.
Stiff hair from a horse’s mane or tail, used to stuff cushions and to weave a scratchy upholstery fabric.
Coaxing or flattering, in order to get one’s way.
A wise adviser. In Homer’s Odyssey, Mentor is the friend who guides young Telemachus.
French for a match: a person considered a good catch for marriage, usually because of wealth or position.
A state of deep offense or resentment.
To take paid work in someone else’s household, as a servant, nurse or the like.
A house where lodgers pay for a room and meals, often eaten together at a common table.
Young men showed interest by calling at a young woman’s home, escorting her to events or sending flowers. Mothers of daughters watched for wealthy young men who might make a good match.
Light, playful romantic attention without serious intent. Many 19th-century moralists disapproved of it, especially in girls, as unkind and unladylike.

Respectable paid work for a middle-class woman in the 1860s was limited: teaching, governessing, sewing, nursing, writing or acting as a lady’s companion. Taking a post in another family’s household could feel like a step down in status.
The English Romantic poet (1788–1824), as famous for his scandalous life as for his poems. His brooding, passionate heroes made gloom fashionable among young men.
A rousing song by Walter Scott about the Jacobite leader Viscount Dundee riding out in 1689. Its chorus, about the “bonnets of bonnie Dundee,” made it a favorite to sing or whistle.

An English bat-and-ball game played between two teams of eleven. Batsmen score runs and can be out by being caught or “stumped,” and its jargon baffles outsiders. It was played at some American colleges in the 19th century.
The ancient classical language of India, used here as a byword for something completely unintelligible.

quiz.q: What was troubling Mrs. March about Beth at the start of the chapter?
o: Her cough had come back in the cold
Her spirits, more than her health
She had stopped playing her piano
She was eating almost nothing
quiz.e: “It’s not her health that troubles me now; it’s her spirits.” Beth sat alone, cried over the babies and sang only sad songs.

quiz.q: What did Beth say, watching someone pass beneath the window, that gave Jo her “clue”?
o: “I wish he would come in more often.”
“He never looks up at our window now.”
“He sings better than anyone I know.”
“How strong and well and happy he looks.”
quiz.e: Beth said, “How strong and well and happy that dear boy looks,” then a tear fell on the window-ledge, and Jo concluded, “Beth loves Laurie!”

quiz.q: What did it mean when “the sausage” lay flat across the sofa?
o: Laurie wasn’t to sit next to Jo
Jo was in the middle of a story
Beth wanted to lie down and rest
The girls were going out that night
quiz.e: If Jo’s hard horsehair pillow stood on end, Laurie might sit beside her; lying flat, it barred him from the seat he most coveted.

quiz.q: When Laurie said his feelings “must have a went,” what did Jo advise?
o: To pour them into his music instead
To save them for his college studies
To devote himself to a modest girl he respected
To go abroad and forget the silly girls
quiz.e: Jo told him to give his attention to one of the “pretty, modest girls” he respected, though preferably after college. Laurie asked, with an odd look, “You really advise it?”

quiz.q: That night, when Jo asked whether Beth was crying from “the old pain,” what did Beth answer?
o: It was a new pain, but she could bear it
It was the old pain, only much worse
She had dreamed about Amy at sea
She was only cold and could not get to sleep
quiz.e: “No; it’s a new one; but I can bear it.” She begged Jo not to call their mother and promised to explain “by and by.”

quiz.q: What work did Jo propose to take up in New York?
o: Writing for a city newspaper
Studying at a ladies’ seminary
Teaching and sewing for Mrs. Kirke
Nursing the sick in a large city hospital
quiz.e: Mrs. Kirke, a friend of Marmee’s who kept a boardinghouse, had asked for a respectable young person to teach her children and sew.

quiz.q: What deeper reason did Jo finally give her mother for wanting to go away?
o: She wanted to earn money for Beth
Aunt March had urged her to leave
She was tired of nursing the babies
She feared Laurie was too fond of her
quiz.e: “I’m afraid—Laurie is getting too fond of me.” Mrs. March agreed they were too alike, with hot tempers and strong wills, to be happy married.

quiz.q: What did Jo leave to Beth’s “especial care” the night before she left?
o: Her stories and papers
Her boy, Laurie
The kittens and birds
Their father’s study
quiz.e: Beth guessed Jo meant her papers, but Jo meant “my boy,” to “plague, pet, and keep in order”; Beth wondered why Jo looked at her so queerly.

chapters.title: Jo’s Journal
chapters.intro: Background on German culture in America, city boarding life, and some literary references, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: A joking name for a small room at the top of a house, an attic room.
A container for carrying coal, usually a deep metal bucket with a handle.
Extremely poor. The saying goes that a church has no food in it for a mouse.
Here, a school, especially a private school for girls.
Flirtatious in a playful, showy way.
French for “terrible child”: a child who embarrasses adults by saying exactly what they think.
As a verb in the 19th century: to tease or make fun of someone.
To mend a hole in knitted cloth, such as a sock, by weaving yarn across it with a needle.
In German folklore, a mischievous household sprite or goblin.
A tobacco pipe with a bowl carved from meerschaum, a soft white mineral.
A bag for scraps of cloth saved for mending or patchwork.
German for fairy tales or folk tales.
An inkstand, a stand holding ink, pens and other writing things.
Love of fine art objects; “an article of vertu” is a curio or ornament kept for display.
A rich, heavy fabric woven with raised patterns, often in silk with gold or silver thread.
A young person regarded as impertinent or self-important.

Huge numbers of Germans came to the United States in the mid-19th century, some of them educated liberals who left after the failed revolutions of 1848. Many earned their living in American cities by teaching languages and music.
In Germany the title “Professor” belonged to a university teacher and carried real dignity. The University of Berlin was among the most respected in Europe.
“Knowest thou the land where the lemon trees bloom?” A song of longing from Goethe’s novel Wilhelm Meister’s Apprenticeship, set to music by many composers.
The Danish writer (1805–1875) of fairy tales such as “The Little Mermaid,” “The Ugly Duckling” and “The Steadfast Tin Soldier,” widely read in German and English translation.
In German and Dutch folklore, storks nesting on a chimney bring good luck to the house, and they are said to bring babies.
The earthy, unruly squire of Don Quixote in Cervantes’s novel; acting “like Sancho” means being disorderly and unmanageable.
A Roman town buried with Pompeii by the eruption of Vesuvius in AD 79. It is easily confused with “Herculean,” meaning requiring the strength of Hercules.

A character in Richard Brinsley Sheridan’s comedy The Rivals (1775) who constantly uses the wrong word, as in “a nice derangement of epitaphs” for “a nice arrangement of epithets.” A misused word is still called a malapropism.
In Shakespeare’s A Midsummer Night’s Dream, Nick Bottom is a weaver given a donkey’s head by magic, and Titania is the fairy queen who is enchanted into loving him.
Many people in 1860s New York, from clerks to whole families, lived in boardinghouses, eating together at a long table. Meals came at set hours, with dinner often in the late afternoon.
Letters were charged by weight, so long letters written on thin paper in a small hand saved money on stamps.

quiz.q: How did Jo keep from crying on the journey to New York?
o: By reading Amy’s latest letter
By sketching her fellow passengers in pencil
By starting her journal-letter
By feeding gingerbread to crying children
quiz.e: An Irish lady with four crying children sat nearby, and Jo dropped gingerbread nuts over the seat every time they opened their mouths to roar.

quiz.q: What kind act first made Jo notice Professor Bhaer?
o: Paying a newsboy for a lost paper
Giving up his seat at the dinner table
Carrying a coal hod for a young servant
Mending a doll for one of the Kirke girls
quiz.e: He took a heavy hod of coal from a little servant girl and carried it upstairs: “The little back is too young to haf such heaviness.”

quiz.q: Who was little Tina?
o: Professor Bhaer’s own daughter
The child of the house’s French laundress
Mrs. Kirke’s youngest little girl
The orphaned niece of Miss Norton
quiz.e: Jo first guessed Tina was Bhaer’s own child, but she was the daughter of the Frenchwoman who did the fine ironing, and she followed him about the house.

quiz.q: What did Jo overhear two young men say about her at the hall mirror?
o: “Handsome head, but no style.”
“Pretty face, but far too tall.”
“Clever enough, but very plain.”
“Well dressed, but very stiff.”
quiz.e: Jo was angry at first, then decided she had sense, if not style, “which is more than some people have.”

quiz.q: When Jo knocked Professor Bhaer’s door open with her umbrella, what was he doing?
o: Playing on his old flute
Rigging a little toy boat
Darning a big blue sock
Feeding his white mice
quiz.e: He stood in his dressing gown with a sock on one hand and a darning-needle in the other, and waved them cheerfully: “Bon voyage, mademoiselle.”

quiz.q: Why did Professor Bhaer insist on giving Jo German lessons?
o: Mrs. Kirke had asked him to teach her
To repay her for secretly mending his things
She needed German for her writing work
He was short of one more paying pupil
quiz.e: He had noticed that his sock-heels no longer had holes and his buttons “grow out new”: “I haf this debt to pay.”

quiz.q: What new method finally got Jo’s German lessons going well?
o: Reciting Goethe’s poems by heart
Talking German together at dinner
Studying alongside little Tina
Reading Andersen’s fairy tales
quiz.e: After Jo stuck fast in a “grammatical bog,” Bhaer threw the grammar on the floor and opened Hans Andersen; the grammar got “tucked into the tales” like pills in jelly.

quiz.q: What did Professor Bhaer give Jo on New Year’s Day?
o: His own treasured Shakespeare
A new German dictionary
A volume of Andersen’s tales
His well-worn copy of Plato
quiz.e: He gave her the Shakespeare he valued, inscribed “from my friend Friedrich Bhaer,” saying its study of character would help her “paint it with your pen.”

chapters.title: A Friend
chapters.intro: Background on popular fiction and publishing in the 1860s, moral tales, and some literary and philosophical references, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: A daydream or hope with little chance of coming true.
French for “castle in Spain,” meaning the same as a castle in the air.
A sleeveless apron-like garment worn over a dress, especially by children.
Short for manuscript, an author’s handwritten copy of a work.
A pen name: a false name an author writes under.
Bandits, especially the picturesque robbers of Italian romance (an old plural of “bandit”).
A writer who turns out large amounts of ordinary work to order, for pay.
To spoil or treat with disrespect something sacred or precious.
Having an unhealthy interest in gloomy or gruesome things.
Originally a Greek drinking party with conversation; here, a gathering for learned or literary talk.
As a noun: a clergyman or theologian.
French for “disillusioned” (of a woman): having lost one’s illusions.
The branch of philosophy that asks about the basic nature of reality, being and knowledge.
Intended to teach or to give moral instruction.
A joking phrase for money, from the New Testament.
A reception at which a person receives visitors, originally a monarch’s morning reception.

A wildly popular kind of fiction in the 1860s, full of crime, poison, madness, secret identities and dark passions, designed to thrill. Critics and moralists considered it cheap and harmful, especially for the young.
Cheap weekly newspapers filled with serial fiction sold in huge numbers. Editors paid writers little, often by the column, and many stories appeared anonymously or under invented names.
Mrs. Mary Martha Sherwood, Maria Edgeworth and Hannah More were British writers of the late 1700s and early 1800s known for improving, instructive stories and tracts for children and the poor.
Religious publishers flooded the market with pious stories for children in which good children were rewarded, often by a holy death, and naughty ones came to dreadful ends.
The fairy tale in which Jack climbs a magic beanstalk to a giant’s castle, steals treasures, and narrowly escapes the giant each time.
Thomas Carlyle’s strange philosophical book (1833–34), whose title means “the tailor retailored.” It treats clothes as symbols of how society and custom cover human life.

Germaine de Staël (1766–1817) was a brilliant French writer and famous conversationalist. Her novel Corinne (1807) tells of a gifted woman poet; both names came to stand for a dazzling literary woman.

Immanuel Kant and G. W. F. Hegel, German philosophers whose difficult systems, about how the mind knows the world, shaped 19th-century thought. Talk of the “Subjective” and “Objective” came from this tradition.
Friedrich Schiller’s trilogy of plays (1799) about a great general of the Thirty Years’ War; the last part is The Death of Wallenstein.

quiz.q: How did Jo explain the story she brought to Mr. Dashwood?
o: She said a friend had written it
She said it was a German translation
She said her father had sent it
She said a teacher had asked for it
quiz.e: She stammered that “a friend of mine desired me to offer—a story,” and the knowing glances of the men in the office showed that her fiction was taken as a joke.

quiz.q: What had Mr. Dashwood struck out of Jo’s story?
o: The love scenes
The descriptions of Italy
All the moral reflections
The whole closing chapter
quiz.e: Jo had put in moral reflections “as ballast for much romance.” Dashwood told her, “People want to be amused, not preached at… Morals don’t sell nowadays.”

quiz.q: What name did Jo choose to have printed with her stories?
o: Her own full name
No name at all
Her initials only
A French pen name
quiz.e: “She doesn’t wish her name to appear, and has no nom de plume.” With no name printed, it was easy to keep her secret from home.

quiz.q: What was Jo saving her earnings for?
o: Amy’s painting lessons in Rome
A new carpet for the parlor
A gift for Laurie’s graduation
Taking Beth to the mountains
quiz.e: Her “little hoard” was to take Beth to the mountains the next summer, but she did not tell her family, feeling her parents would not approve.

quiz.q: Which of these did Jo do in search of thrilling material?
o: Asked librarians for works on poisons
Visited the jail to talk to prisoners
Questioned sailors along the docks
Sat through murder trials at court
quiz.e: She searched newspapers for crimes and “excited the suspicions of public librarians by asking for works on poisons.”

quiz.q: What did Jo decide was the secret of Professor Bhaer’s charm?
o: His great learning
His fund of stories
His fine deep voice
His benevolence
quiz.e: She concluded that “genuine goodwill towards one’s fellow-men could beautify and dignify even a stout German teacher.”

quiz.q: What did Jo learn about the Professor through Miss Norton?
o: He had been wealthy in Germany
He had once served as a soldier
He had been honored in Berlin
He had published his own poems
quiz.e: A visiting countryman revealed that Bhaer had been an honored professor in Berlin; Jo liked it all the better because he had never told it himself.

quiz.q: What did Professor Bhaer do when appealed to at the philosophers’ gathering?
o: Turned the talk to music and art
Defended religion against them
Agreed politely with the speakers
Took Jo home without a word
quiz.e: Usually slow to give opinions, he “blazed up with honest indignation” and defended religion; Jo felt she had solid ground under her feet again.

quiz.q: After the Professor burned the sensational paper, what did Jo do with her own stories?
o: Burned them all in her stove
Sent them back to Mr. Dashwood
Locked them away in her trunk
Mailed them home to Marmee
quiz.e: Rereading them “through the Professor’s spectacles,” she called them trash and stuffed the whole bundle into her stove, nearly setting the chimney afire.

quiz.q: As her train left in June, what did Jo think she had gained from the winter?
o: A novel ready to sell
A fortune for home
A friend worth having
A command of German
quiz.e: “I’ve written no books, earned no fortune; but I’ve made a friend worth having, and I’ll try to keep him all my life.”

chapters.title: Heartache
chapters.intro: Background on college commencement, famous orators, and some music and Shakespeare, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: A formal speech given on a ceremonial occasion.
A small, simple instrument held between the teeth and twanged with a finger to make a buzzing tune.
French for “head to head”: a private conversation between two people.
A large bottle with a narrow neck, usually encased in wicker.
Steps or a step-over built into a fence or wall so people can climb over while animals cannot.
The quality of acting suddenly and rashly, without thinking.
To dig in and take up a strong defensive position, in argument as in war.
In American usage: plain or unattractive in appearance.
Too old for work or use; retired because of age.
Someone who spoils a plan by meddling. The word comes from a character in an 18th-century comedy.
To go from place to place in search of amusement.
Deep in serious, often sad, thought.
Not returned. Unrequited love is love that is not returned.
Anxious care and concern for someone.
The ceremony at which American college students receive their degrees, usually held in early summer and attended by proud families.
Older American colleges kept the custom of having an outstanding student deliver an oration in Latin at commencement, a mark of high academic standing.
Students with the best records received honors at graduation and were often chosen to speak at the ceremony.
The great orator of ancient Athens (384–322 BC), long held up as the model of eloquence.
An American abolitionist (1811–1884) famous as one of the most graceful and powerful public speakers of his day.
A triumphant chorus by Handel, used for generations to welcome a victor home, often misquoted as “Hail the conquering hero comes.”
Beethoven’s Piano Sonata No. 8 in C minor, nicknamed “Pathétique,” a dramatic, deeply emotional work, much loved by amateur pianists.
A comedy by Shakespeare in which young men’s courtships come to nothing at the end. The title became a phrase for effort that is wasted.

quiz.q: What did Laurie deliver at his college commencement?
o: The class poem
A Greek recitation
The Latin oration
The farewell address
quiz.e: He graduated with honor and gave the Latin oration “with the grace of a Phillips and the eloquence of a Demosthenes, so his friends said.”

quiz.q: What did Jo jokingly promise to do when she met Laurie the next day?
o: Play “Hail the conquering hero” on a jews-harp
Crown him with a wreath of laurel from the garden
Read him a comic ode she had written in his honor
Bring Meg’s babies along to cheer for the graduate
quiz.e: She promised to “march before you, playing ‘Hail the conquering hero comes,’ on a jews-harp”; when they met, she had forgotten it.

quiz.q: What did Laurie say he had given up in the hope of pleasing Jo?
o: His horses and his rowing
The theater and late suppers
His music and his friends
Billiards and all she disliked
quiz.e: “I gave up billiards and everything you didn’t like, and waited and never complained, for I hoped you’d love me.”

quiz.q: When Jo said she wanted to tell him something, whom did Laurie fear she would say she loved?
o: Fred Vaughn
Professor Bhaer
Ned Moffat
Mr. Dashwood
quiz.e: “That devilish Professor you were always writing about.” Jo first thought “that old man” meant Laurie’s grandfather.

quiz.q: Agreeing with her mother, why did Jo say she and Laurie were not suited?
o: Their quick tempers and strong wills
The great difference in their fortunes
Her duty to stay at home with Beth
His youth and his want of a profession
quiz.e: She argued their “quick tempers and strong wills” would make them miserable, and added that she loved her liberty too well to marry.

quiz.q: After crying “To the devil!”, where did Laurie go?
o: Off at a gallop on his horse
Down the road to the station
Up to his room at the house
Off up the river in his boat
quiz.e: He flung his hat and coat into his boat and rowed away with all his might, “making better time up the river than he had done in many a race.”

quiz.q: What broke off Laurie’s playing at the piano that evening?
o: His grandfather closing the piano lid
Hearing Mrs. March call Jo inside
Beth beginning to sing in the garden
A string snapping in the middle of it
quiz.e: Mrs. March called, “Jo, dear, come in; I want you”—just what Laurie longed to say. He lost his place and the music ended on a broken chord.

quiz.q: What plan did Mr. Laurence propose to his grandson?
o: To start work at once under Brooke
To study alone at a German university
To go abroad with him, on London business
To spend the summer with friends at the shore
quiz.e: Mr. Laurence would see to business in London and visit friends there and in Paris, leaving Laurie free to roam Italy, Germany and Switzerland.

chapters.title: Beth’s Secret
chapters.intro: Background on seaside holidays, shore birds and Christian ideas of patience, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: Persuaded, after some effort, to do something.
A habit of holding back one’s feelings or not speaking openly about them.
Quietly sad and longing, often for something out of reach.
An affectionate pet name, like “dear” or “darling.”
Pining or unhappy because of love that is not returned. “Love-lornity” is a playful made-up noun from it.
In a defiant way, refusing to accept something.
In a deeply religious, devout way.
Ready to accept and give in to authority or circumstances.
A sermon or moral lecture, especially a long or tedious one.
A strong, solemn declaration of a feeling or belief.
To criticize or scold someone sharply.
Gradually separated from something one has depended on, as a baby from its mother’s milk.
A popular name for small sandpipers, little gray-brown shorebirds named for their thin, piping call.
Plain gray or drab, like the simple clothing worn by Quakers.
A small, soft-voiced dove, long a symbol of gentle and faithful love.

By the mid-1800s, New England families of modest means often spent quiet weeks at the coast, lodging in simple boarding houses rather than grand hotels. Fashionable resorts drew the wealthy; plainer places drew those seeking rest.
Nineteenth-century doctors often prescribed fresh sea air, mountain air and time outdoors for people in weak health, believing a change of air could strengthen the body when medicines could not.
Gulls are large, strong seabirds that range far over the water. Sandpipers are small, quick shorebirds that run along the tide line, picking food from the wet sand.
The skylark is famous for singing as it climbs high into the sky, then dropping back to the ground where it nests. Poets, including Shelley in “To a Skylark,” made it a symbol of joy and aspiration.
A phrase from the Gospels, where Jesus tells his followers to take up their cross and follow him. It came to mean accepting one’s hardships patiently and without complaint.
Many nineteenth-century New England Protestants valued quiet goodness in daily life over talk about religion, and admired people whose faith showed in their kindness rather than their words.
People of the period often found it hard to speak openly about health or deep feelings, even within families, and might keep painful matters to themselves to spare others worry.

quiz.q: What struck Jo about Beth when she came home that spring?
o: Beth had grown restless and talked of travel
Beth’s face had a strange, transparent look
Beth had become cross and short with everyone
Beth seemed rosier and stronger than in autumn
quiz.e: Her face was “no paler and but little thinner,” yet it had a transparent look, “as if the mortal was being slowly refined away.”

quiz.q: When Jo offered her savings for a mountain trip, what did Beth ask for instead?
o: A trip to New York with Jo
A long visit to Aunt March
Lessons on a new grand piano
Another visit to the seashore
quiz.e: Beth begged not to go far from home; “another little visit to the seashore would suit her better.”

quiz.q: Why did only Jo and Beth go to the seashore?
o: Their mother would not leave the babies
Their father was too busy with his books
Meg needed Jo’s help with the household
Hannah could not be spared from the house
quiz.e: “Grandma could not be prevailed upon to leave the babies,” so Jo took Beth to the quiet place by herself.

quiz.q: When did Beth say she had given up hoping to get well?
o: When Amy first sailed away to Europe
At Christmas, after Meg’s twins were born
In the autumn, when she was so unhappy
Last summer, when she first came to the shore
quiz.e: Jo had wondered what made Beth so unhappy in the autumn; Beth explains, “Yes, I gave up hoping then, but I didn’t like to own it.”

quiz.q: What had Jo mistakenly believed about Beth?
o: That Beth was in love with Laurie
That Beth longed to go abroad like Amy
That Beth was jealous of Amy’s trip
That Beth was angry with Jo for leaving
quiz.e: Jo confesses she went away partly because she thought Beth loved Laurie; Beth is amazed, saying he could never be anything to her but a brother.

quiz.q: To what does Beth compare her slow loss of strength?
o: A candle burning down
The tide going out
A leaf in the autumn
A clock running down
quiz.e: “It’s like the tide, Jo, when it turns, it goes slowly, but it can’t be stopped.”

quiz.q: In Beth’s comparison of the sisters to birds, which bird is Jo?
o: The lark
The turtledove
The little sand-bird
The gull
quiz.e: Jo is the gull, “strong and wild, fond of the storm and the wind”; Meg is the turtledove, Amy the lark, and Beth herself the little “peeps.”

quiz.q: What happened when the sisters got home?
o: Jo told her parents everything that evening
Beth herself broke the news at breakfast
Her parents saw the truth without being told
Meg guessed it first and told her mother
quiz.e: No words were needed: Jo found her father leaning his head on the mantelpiece and her mother stretching out her arms to her for comfort.

chapters.title: New Impressions
chapters.intro: Background on the French Riviera, famous names of the 1860s and ballroom customs, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: A wide public walk, often by the sea, where people stroll to see and be seen.
A carriage together with its horses and servants; a fashionable turnout.
A light four-wheeled carriage with a folding hood. A “basket” barouche had a wicker body.
A man who pays great attention to fine and showy clothes.
A long, thin candle, often carried in religious processions.
Bored or unimpressed, from having seen or enjoyed too much.
Self-confidence and poise, especially in company.
To dress up carefully and fussily before a mirror.
A thin, stiff, open-weave cotton fabric used for ball gowns.
A fine, light netting of silk or cotton used for veils and skirts.
A lady’s outfit or style of dress; also the business of dressing.
A very fine, transparent silk net used to cover or trim gowns.
A gliding dance step in which one foot seems to chase the other.
A small bunch of flowers, often carried at a ball.
A social dance with set figures performed by groups of couples; also spelled cotillion.
To dance the galop, a lively round dance in quick time.
A city on the Mediterranean coast, part of the Kingdom of Sardinia until 1860, when it passed to France. Its mild winters drew wealthy visitors from all over Europe and America.
Nice’s famous seafront walk, whose name means “the English promenade”; it was named for the English visitors who wintered in the town.
A large, mountainous Mediterranean island lying south-east of Nice, famous as the birthplace of Napoleon Bonaparte.

Adelaide Ristori was a celebrated Italian tragic actress; Charles Dickens was the best-known English novelist; Victor Emmanuel II became the first king of a united Italy in 1861; the Sandwich Islands was the old English name for Hawaii, then an independent kingdom.
In Roman myth, Diana is the goddess of the hunt and the moon and Apollo the god of the sun, music and poetry; they are twins, and both were favorite subjects for classical statues.
Hebe was the Greek goddess of youth, often shown with her hair in a simple knot. Juno was the stately queen of the Roman gods, so a “Junoesque” woman is tall and majestic.
Lines from Tennyson’s poem “A Dream of Fair Women,” describing a woman “divinely tall, and most divinely fair.”
Honoré de Balzac was a great French novelist of the early 1800s. Mr. Pickwick, hero of Dickens’s first novel, is a stout, bald, endlessly cheerful old gentleman.
Young ladies at balls carried small cards or books in which partners wrote their names for each dance in advance. Being “engaged” for a dance meant it was already promised.
Ballrooms mixed stately figure dances like the cotillion with quick round dances such as the polka, the redowa (a Bohemian dance) and the galop.
A young unmarried woman was expected to attend balls with an older lady, her chaperon, who sat by the wall and watched over her between dances.
In the 1860s growing numbers of well-off Americans traveled and wintered in Europe, especially France and Italy, often mixing freely with titled Europeans.

quiz.q: Where is Laurie walking on Christmas Day when the chapter opens?
o: Down a wide boulevard in Paris
Beside the harbor at Genoa
Along the promenade at Nice
Through a park in Berlin
quiz.e: At three in the afternoon “all the fashionable world at Nice” is on the Promenade des Anglais, where Laurie spots a blonde girl in blue driving her ponies.

quiz.q: Where did Laurie say his grandfather had settled for the winter?
o: In Paris
In Berlin
In London
In Rome
quiz.e: Laurie spent a month in Berlin, then joined his grandfather in Paris: “he hates to travel, and I hate to keep still.”

quiz.q: What did Amy notice about Laurie as they waited for the procession to pass?
o: He seemed restless and eager to leave Nice
He was thinner and seemed to be unwell
He had grown loud and boastful in his talk
He looked tired, older and graver than before
quiz.e: She could not find “the merry-faced boy” in “the moody-looking man beside her,” who looked “older and graver” than prosperous years should have made him.

quiz.q: Why did Laurie’s polished compliment fail to please Amy?
o: She suspected he was mocking her French
It sounded cool, unlike his old praise
She feared her aunt would think it bold
It was the very thing he had said to Flo
quiz.e: She missed the “blunt praises” he gave her at home, when he told her she was “altogether jolly”; the new tone “sounded indifferent.”

quiz.q: How does Laurie greet Amy when he finds her waiting in her white dress?
o: “Good evening, Juno!”
“Good evening, Hebe!”
“Good evening, Venus!”
“Good evening, Diana!”
quiz.e: “Good evening, Diana!” he says; she answers, “Good evening, Apollo!”

quiz.q: What gift did Laurie bring Amy before the ball?
o: A nosegay in a holder she had long coveted
A silver fan to match her rosy azaleas
A pair of white satin dancing slippers
A string of pearls from a Paris jeweler
quiz.e: He arranged the flowers himself, remembering her dislike of a “sot-bookay,” and put them in a holder she had admired daily in Cardiglia’s window.

quiz.q: What did Amy do when Laurie strolled, rather than rushed, to claim a later dance?
o: She refused to speak to him all night
She complained to her aunt about him
She showed him her full ball-book
She danced it with him after all
quiz.e: Having engaged herself till supper, she showed him her ball-book “with demure satisfaction” and gallopaded away with the Polish Count.

quiz.q: How did Laurie spend the rest of the evening after supper?
o: He left early to write to his grandfather
He filled her book and stayed by her side
He danced every remaining dance with Flo
He sat talking politics with Mrs. Carrol
quiz.e: Admiring “the cheerful spirit that covered poverty with flowers,” he filled up her book with his own name and devoted himself to her.

chapters.title: On the Shelf
chapters.intro: Background on married life, households and the place of women in the 1860s, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: A married woman, especially one settled into family life.
To give up a throne or a position of power.
Hired household servants, such as cooks and maids.
A small errand or task given to someone to do.
A newspaper column listing ships’ arrivals, departures and cargoes.
The area within the boundaries of a place, often a sacred or private one.
A low metal frame in front of a fireplace that keeps coals from rolling out.
A burden or responsibility, often used jokingly of children; also spelled encumbrance.
To make hair wavy or curled, often with heated irons.
Gentle, obedient and easy to teach.
A light round box for hats or collars; to live “in a bandbox” is to be kept shut away and too delicate for the world.
Stubbornly determined; refusing to give up.
A person who spoils a plan by meddling.
A long, forceful speech or lecture.
Women’s hats and their trimmings, or the trade of making them.
An old expression for someone set aside as no longer wanted or noticed, most often said of a woman thought too old to marry.
Many Americans of the period held that men belonged to the world of business and politics and women to the home, where they were expected to devote themselves to husband and children.
Women could not vote in national elections in the 1860s, and many were discouraged from following politics, though newspapers printed long reports of debates and elections.
Large numbers of Irish immigrants arrived in America in the mid-1800s, and many young Irish women found work as cooks and maids in middle-class homes.
Nineteenth-century parents greatly feared teething, which was blamed for fevers, sleeplessness and illness in babies.
A respectable woman wore a bonnet out of doors, tied under the chin. Small, lacy bonnets for concerts and the theatre were fashionable in the 1860s.
From the nursery rhyme “Humpty Dumpty,” where all the king’s horses and men cannot put the fallen egg together again; used of anything that cannot be changed.
A saying from the First Epistle of Peter in the New Testament, meaning that love overlooks faults.
From the last lines of Coleridge’s poem “The Rime of the Ancient Mariner,” describing someone chastened by hard experience.
The word comes from old words meaning the master of a household. Writers sometimes punned on it as the “house-band” that binds a home together.

quiz.q: Where did John begin spending his evenings when home became “merely a nursery”?
o: At the Laurences’ house
At his club in the town
At the Moffats’ house
At the Scotts’ house
quiz.e: Scott had married and settled nearby; Mrs. Scott’s parlor always had the chessboard ready, gay gossip and a nice little supper.

quiz.q: When Meg complained that men are selfish, what did her mother reply?
o: That John simply needed a holiday
That women are too, and Meg was at fault
That Meg should speak to John at once
That Mrs. Scott was a poor influence
quiz.e: “So are women; don’t blame John till you see where you are wrong yourself.” Marmee then asks, “Don’t you neglect him?”

quiz.q: What did Marmee say had happened when Meg and Jo were little?
o: Father was away and she managed everything alone
Aunt March took over the care of both girls
She refused father’s help until he stepped in
Hannah ran the house while she nursed Beth
quiz.e: She devoted herself wholly to the children, nearly spoiled Jo and fell sick herself, until father “came to the rescue” and she saw her mistake.

quiz.q: Which plan did Marmee suggest to Meg?
o: Let Hannah help with the babies
Send the twins to stay with her
Hire a second, better cook
Take a long rest at the seaside
quiz.e: Hannah, “a capital nurse,” could mind the babies while Meg did more housework, and John should have more to do with managing Demi.

quiz.q: What spoiled the start of Meg’s planned evening with John?
o: Daisy fell ill with a cold
Demi refused to stay in bed
Kitty burned the nice supper
The Scotts called unexpectedly
quiz.e: Demi’s “most unconquerable prejudice was against going to bed,” and he soon appeared at the door: “Opy doy; me’s tummin!”

quiz.q: How did Meg first coax Demi back to bed?
o: She sang him a long lullaby
She let Daisy lie beside him
She left the lamp burning for him
She gave him a lump of sugar
quiz.e: “That shortsighted woman actually gave him a lump of sugar,” and he soon returned demanding “More sudar, marmar.”

quiz.q: What did Meg find when she slipped into the nursery after the long silence?
o: Father and son both fast asleep
Demi crying alone in the dark
John telling Demi a story by the fire
Demi asleep with the lamp burning
quiz.e: Demi lay in “a subdued bunch,” cuddled in his father’s arm and holding his finger; John had fallen asleep while waiting.

quiz.q: What did John mistake Meg’s new bonnet for?
o: A pincushion
A lampshade
A breakfast-cap
A doll’s bonnet
quiz.e: “My dear man, it’s a bonnet! My very best go-to-concert-and-theatre bonnet.” He decides to like millinery for her sake, as she tries to like politics for his.

chapters.title: Lazy Laurence
chapters.intro: Background on the Riviera countryside, classical and saintly references, and travel customs, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: To waste time; to move or act slowly and idly.
A drawing room or reception room, especially in a French house or hotel.
Gloves made of fine, soft leather from young goats.
One of a pair of baskets slung across the back of a donkey or horse.
A broad-brimmed sun hat worn by country women in the south of France.
A stick that holds wool or flax while it is spun into thread by hand.
A small cave, often an artificial one in a garden, decorated with shells or statues.
A decorative molding running along the top of a wall or building.
A railing supported by a row of short pillars, as along a terrace.
A daydream; being lost in one’s thoughts.
A carved figure of a person, such as the stone image lying on top of a tomb.
Lack of interest, feeling or energy.
Lying face upward; also, lazy and inactive.
The southern end of the Alps, rising behind Nice along the border between France and Italy.
A tiny principality on the coast near Nice, famous for its casino.
A German spa town famous in the 1800s for its mineral baths and its gambling casino, which drew rich and fashionable visitors.
Italian for “sweet doing nothing”: the pleasure of idleness.
A deacon of the early Church in Rome, martyred in 258. Tradition says he was roasted on a gridiron and joked with his executioners, so he is often shown holding one.
In Homer’s Odyssey, young Telemachus is guided by Mentor, an old friend of his father (sometimes the goddess Athena in disguise). “Mentor” came to mean a wise, trusted adviser.
A great Italian painter of the High Renaissance; many of his finest works are in Rome.
John S. Rarey was an American horse tamer who became famous in the 1850s for calming wild horses by gentle methods, giving demonstrations in America and Europe.
Well-off young men from Britain and America often spent months or years traveling in Europe after their studies, seeing art, scenery and society.
On the Continent a gentleman might bow to kiss a lady’s hand in greeting or farewell; Americans and English people generally preferred a handshake.

quiz.q: How long did Laurie stay at Nice?
o: A month, though he meant to stay a week
A week, just as he had always planned
Two days, before going to his grandfather
The whole winter, until the spring came
quiz.e: “Laurie went to Nice intending to stay a week, and remained a month,” tired of wandering alone.

quiz.q: What happened when Laurie reached for a scarlet rose at Valrosa?
o: Amy scolded him for spoiling the garden
A gardener came out and sent him off
He pricked his thumb on its thorns
He picked it and gave it to Amy
quiz.e: “No, nor felt such thorns,” he says, thumb in mouth. Amy gives him three thornless cream-colored roses instead, the kind Italians lay in dead hands.

quiz.q: Why had Amy given up her hopes of being a great artist?
o: Her aunt thought painting unladylike
Rome showed her talent isn’t genius
Her teacher said she had no real gift
She had spent her money on lessons
quiz.e: “Rome took all the vanity out of me… talent isn’t genius, and no amount of energy can make it so.” She now means to be “an ornament to society.”

quiz.q: What reasons did Amy give for being willing to marry Fred Vaughn?
o: He loved art and admired her work
He was kind, clever and a fine scholar
His family had long known her own
He was rich, a gentleman, well-mannered
quiz.e: Laurie thinks Fred “not the man I fancied you’d like”; Amy admits she means to make a good match.

quiz.q: What did Amy say when Laurie asked to hear what she honestly thought of him?
o: “I pity you”
“I hate you”
“I despise you”
“I fear for you”
quiz.e: Her grave tone stung more than a petulant “I hate you” would have: she calls him selfish, lazy and miserable despite “every chance for being good.”

quiz.q: What on Laurie’s hand helped Amy guess the cause of his change?
o: The little old ring Jo gave him
A heavy seal-ring set with a stone
An ink stain from writing poems
A scar from taming the horse Puck
quiz.e: She recalled that he never spoke of Jo and still wore “the little old one Jo gave you so long ago,” and was sure a love trouble lay behind it.

quiz.q: Whom did Amy pretend to blame, to be sure of her facts?
o: Flo Carrol
Miss Randal
Fred Vaughn
Sallie Moffat
quiz.e: “I never did like that Miss Randal, and now I hate her!” Laurie bursts out that he never cared for anyone but Jo.

quiz.q: What did Laurie’s note the next morning tell Amy?
o: He had gone to Vienna to study music
He would call that evening as usual
He had sailed for home to see Jo
He had gone to join his grandfather
quiz.e: Signed “Telemachus” to his “dear Mentor,” it said “Lazy Laurence” had gone to his grandpa “like the best of boys.”

chapters.title: The Valley of the Shadow
chapters.intro: Background on Bible and Pilgrim’s Progress references, home nursing and schoolroom life in the 1800s, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: This chapter includes serious illness and a death.
A journey made out of devotion, often to a holy place.
A person made weak by illness, often confined to bed or to the house.
A holy place, often holding a sacred object or the image of a saint.
A small fabric case with flannel pages for keeping sewing needles.
A small pad of cloth for wiping ink off a pen nib.
Curved strokes that children practiced when learning to write.
To pass time pleasantly; also, to charm.
To gradually separate oneself from something one has depended on.
To leave something to someone, as in a will.
Blessed and radiant, like a saint.
A phrase from Psalm 23: “Yea, though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil.” The psalm has long been read for comfort in times of grief.
In Bunyan’s The Pilgrim’s Progress, pilgrims must cross a deep river before reaching the Celestial City, where angels called the Shining Ones welcome them on the far side.
“Smell sweet, and blossom in the dust”
An echo of the seventeenth-century English poet James Shirley, who wrote that “only the actions of the just” smell sweet and blossom in their dust: good deeds outlive the doer.
In the 1800s the seriously ill were nearly always cared for at home by their families, who took turns sitting up through the night and kept the sickroom fire burning.
Schoolchildren learned to write with steel or quill pens dipped in ink, copying rows of strokes and loops, so blots and inky fingers were part of every lesson.
Small white flowers that bloom at the very end of winter, often through snow, and are among the first signs of spring.

quiz.q: What was done with the pleasantest room in the house?
o: It was made into Jo’s study
It was set apart for Beth
It was kept for Amy’s return
It became Father’s library
quiz.e: Her favorite things gathered there: flowers, pictures, her piano, the pussies, father’s best books and Amy’s finest sketches.

quiz.q: How did John show his kindness to Beth?
o: He set aside money to keep her in fruit
He read aloud to her every evening
He built a new bookcase for her room
He brought a doctor out from the city
quiz.e: “John quietly set apart a little sum” so that the invalid could have the fruit she loved and longed for.

quiz.q: What did Beth do for the schoolchildren who passed her window?
o: Taught them music on her piano
Wrote them cheerful little letters each day
Gave them lessons in reading
Dropped small homemade gifts to them
quiz.e: Mittens, needle-books, pen-wipers and scrapbooks came down from the window, and the children sent back letters “full of blots and gratitude.”

quiz.q: What sign marked the end of the first, happy months?
o: Beth could no longer play her piano
Beth asked to see the doctor daily
Beth said the needle was “so heavy”
Beth stopped writing to the children
quiz.e: She put the needle down “forever”; talking wearied her, and pain “claimed her for its own.”

quiz.q: Why did Jo never leave Beth’s room?
o: Marmee had fallen ill herself
The doctor had ordered a constant nurse
Hannah was too tired to sit up
Beth felt stronger when Jo was there
quiz.e: After Beth said, “I feel stronger when you are here,” Jo slept on a couch in the room, “jealous of any other nurse.”

quiz.q: Where did Beth find Jo’s poem “My Beth”?
o: In Jo’s writing desk
In her mother’s workbasket
In her old Pilgrim’s Progress
Under her own pillow
quiz.e: Turning the leaves of her old favorite, she found the paper, its lines blurred as if tears had fallen on it.

quiz.q: Why did the poem bring Beth such comfort?
o: It promised she would soon be well again
It showed her life had not been useless
It meant Jo would give up her writing
It told her Amy was coming home soon
quiz.e: Her “one regret had been that she had done so little”; the poem assured her that her life had helped someone.

quiz.q: What did Beth ask Jo to do after she was gone?
o: Take her place with father and mother
Finish the stories she had begun
Look after the schoolchildren for her
Give her piano to Meg’s little twins
quiz.e: “You must take my place, Jo, and be everything to father and mother.” Jo then renounced her old ambition for “a new and better one.”

chapters.title: Learning to Forget
chapters.intro: Background on Vienna’s music, literary references and Lake Geneva, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: An odd, unpredictable notion or action.
Black mourning clothes, especially a widow’s.
A Mass for the dead, or a piece of music written for one.
To distress deeply; to torment the feelings.
So fine and light as to be almost see-through.
Aimless; jumping from one thing to another without a plan.
To “sow one’s wild oats” is to go through a period of reckless pleasure-seeking while young.
French for matches, or twists of paper used to light candles and pipes.
A landing place where boats tie up.
French for living as boarders in a guesthouse, with meals included.
The final outcome or resolution of a story.
Of a boat: to sit level and properly balanced in the water.
Johann Wolfgang von Goethe, the great German poet, wrote many lyric poems and songs drawn from his own joys and sorrows.
The capital of Austria and one of Europe’s great musical cities, home at various times to Mozart, Haydn, Beethoven and Schubert.
A Catholic Mass for the dead. Many composers, Mozart among them, wrote famous musical settings of it.
Bach, Mozart, Beethoven and Mendelssohn were German and Austrian composers whose busts and portraits decorated many music rooms in the 1800s.
A character in Thomas Morton’s 1798 play Speed the Plough who never appears but whose opinion everyone fears; her name came to stand for narrow, conventional respectability.
A gloomy widow in Dickens’s David Copperfield who constantly calls herself “a lone lorn creetur” and dampens everyone’s spirits.
In a parable in Matthew’s Gospel, an enemy sows tares among a farmer’s good wheat; the image stands for evil growing up among good.
Vienna’s great Gothic cathedral, where High Mass, a solemn sung Catholic service, is celebrated.
Vevey (once often spelled Vevay) is a Swiss town on the north shore of Lake Geneva, near Montreux, looking across the water to the Alps of Savoy.
A medieval castle on Lake Geneva near Montreux, where François Bonivard was imprisoned for years in the 1500s; Byron’s poem “The Prisoner of Chillon” made it famous.
Jean-Jacques Rousseau’s 1761 novel Julie, or the New Héloïse is a love story set beside Lake Geneva, partly at the village of Clarens.
Victorians showed grief by wearing black, from full black dress to a black ribbon or a small jet or ebony ornament.

quiz.q: What did Laurie first try to compose in Vienna?
o: A sonata
An opera
A requiem
A symphony
quiz.e: He meant his Requiem to “harrow up Jo’s soul,” but kept humming a dance tune that recalled the stout Frenchman at the Christmas ball.

quiz.q: Why couldn’t Laurie make Jo the heroine of his opera?
o: Her letters made him too angry to write
His grandfather forbade him to use her
She had asked him never to write of her
His memory showed only her funny ways
quiz.e: Memory showed her beating mats with her head in a bandana or barricaded behind the sofa-pillow, and “an irresistible laugh spoilt the pensive picture.”

quiz.q: What did Laurie do after coming home from a Mozart opera?
o: Tore up his music
Wrote to his grandfather
Bought a bust of Mozart
Began a new Requiem
quiz.e: “She is right! Talent isn’t genius,” he said, echoing Amy’s words about Rome.

quiz.q: What did Jo’s answer to Laurie’s letter say?
o: She would think it over until spring
She couldn’t and wouldn’t love him
She would write again when Beth was well
She had promised herself to another man
quiz.e: Wrapped up in Beth, she begged him to be happy with somebody else, and asked him not to tell Amy that Beth was worse.

quiz.q: What did Laurie do with Jo’s letters and the little ring?
o: Locked them in a drawer of his desk
Sent them back to Jo in America
Burned them in his stove that night
Gave them to Amy for safekeeping
quiz.e: He laid the ring with the letters, locked the drawer, and went to High Mass at Saint Stefan’s, “feeling as if there had been a funeral.”

quiz.q: How did Amy answer Fred Vaughn’s proposal?
o: “Yes, thank you”
“No, thank you”
“Ask me in a year”
“Ask my mother”
quiz.e: She found that “something more than money and position” was needed; Fred went to Egypt, and Amy made sure Laurie knew it.

quiz.q: Where did Laurie find Amy after the news of Beth reached them?
o: On the terrace at Valrosa
At her hotel in Nice
In the château garden at Vevay
On the quay at Genoa
quiz.e: Wearing a black ribbon and the ebony cross he gave her, she ran to him: “O Laurie, Laurie, I knew you’d come to me!”

quiz.q: How did Laurie finally propose to Amy?
o: By moonlight in the château garden
In a letter left at the pension
After dinner, in front of her aunt
While they rowed together on the lake
quiz.e: “How well we pull together, don’t we?” “So well that I wish we might always pull in the same boat. Will you, Amy?” “Yes, Laurie.”

chapters.title: All Alone
chapters.intro: Background on Pilgrim’s Progress and moral storybooks, magazine writing of the period and old New England customs, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: Giving up your own wishes and comforts for the sake of others.
Unwilling to give in or accept something.
Made humbler, gentler or more restrained, usually by suffering.
Low spirits; a feeling of hopelessness.
A country pronunciation of “creature,” often used affectionately for a person.
Going out into the woods to gather nuts.
A small weight, such as one tied to the tail of a kite.
Here, plain and self-denying, as if worn to punish vanity.
A short printed pamphlet, usually religious, handed out to persuade people.
A shady shelter of branches or vines, often with a seat.
A sleeveless apron worn over a dress to keep it clean.
The quality in writing that stirs pity or sadness.
Interested mainly in money or gain.
A woman to whom secrets are told.
An attic room just under the roof of a house.
A bag for saving scraps of cloth for mending, patchwork or rugs.
John Bunyan’s 1678 allegory follows Christian on his journey to the Celestial City. On the way he climbs the steep Hill Difficulty and rests in a pleasant arbor halfway up, built for weary pilgrims.

Many nineteenth-century books for young readers held up flawless heroines who gave up worldly pleasures and spent their days doing good, often handing out religious tracts. Readers of the time would have recognized the type at once.
A long pull, a strong pull
“A long pull, a strong pull, and a pull all together” was an old call for united effort, like a crew hauling on a rope or rowing in time.

The American chestnut was once common in New England woods. Its nuts grow inside spiny husks called burrs, which split open in autumn after frost, and gathering them was a favorite outing for children.
Old New England houses often had a garret under the roof for storage and rainy-day play, where families kept trunks and chests of old belongings.
Children’s kites were built at home from light sticks, paper and paste, with a weighted tail to keep them steady in the wind.
Popular American magazines of the period paid authors for short stories and poems, often modestly. A story that pleased readers could bring requests for more from editors.
Newspapers of the time freely copied pieces from one another, so a popular story or poem could travel far beyond the magazine that first printed it.
Providence means God’s care and guidance over human lives. Nineteenth-century Christians often spoke of hardships as lessons or tasks sent by Providence.
In Christian teaching, resignation is the calm acceptance of God’s will in sorrow, as opposed to bitter rebellion against it.

quiz.q: In her first dark days at home, what seems most unfair to Jo?
o: That Meg has a happy home while she has none
That her parents now need her more than ever
That she tries harder than Amy but gets no reward
That her writing has brought her no money
quiz.e: Jo feels that some people get “all sunshine, and some all shadow,” and that she tried more than Amy to be good without any reward.

quiz.q: Who comes to comfort Jo when she wakes at night crying for Beth?
o: Her mother
Hannah
Meg
Her father
quiz.e: Mrs. March, as quick to hear Jo’s sobbing as Jo had been to hear Beth, comforts her with tenderness and her own quiet tears.

quiz.q: What does Jo call her father’s study, where the two of them now talk together?
o: “the chapel of quiet hours”
“the house of good counsel”
“the old confessional”
“the church of one member”
quiz.e: Jo calls it “the church of one member,” and comes out of it with fresh courage and a more submissive spirit.

quiz.q: Who notices Jo taking up Beth’s little household ways and says the Lord will bless her for it?
o: Meg
Hannah
Mrs. March
Aunt March
quiz.e: Hannah squeezes her hand: “You’re determined we shan’t miss that dear lamb ef you can help it.”

quiz.q: Meg says Jo is like what, prickly outside but soft within?
o: A thistle in a hedgerow
A rose with sharp thorns
A chestnut-burr
A hedgehog in the garden
quiz.e: Meg says love will make the rough burr fall off one day; Jo jokes that frost opens chestnut-burrs and she doesn’t care to be “bagged” by boys.

quiz.q: What happens to the little story Jo writes to please her family?
o: She reads it aloud and then hides it in her desk
Her father sends it to a magazine, which pays and asks for more
Meg copies it out as a present for the twins
She sends it to a weekly paper under a false name
quiz.e: Her father sends it off against her will; it is paid for, copied by newspapers and praised by strangers. He tells her she has “found your style at last.”

quiz.q: What does Jo admit to her mother after reading of Amy and Laurie’s engagement?
o: That she had guessed it long before Marmee did
That she still loves Laurie more than she ever said
That she envies Amy’s fine life abroad in Europe
That she is lonely, and might now have said yes
quiz.e: Jo says she might have said “Yes” if Teddy had tried again, not because she loves him more, but because she now cares more to be loved.

quiz.q: What does Jo find in the garret that makes her lips tremble?
o: A note from the Professor in her exercise-books
A faded letter from Laurie hidden in her chest
A little cap of Beth’s folded away in Beth’s chest
A copy of the first story she ever saw in print
quiz.e: The note reads “Wait for me, my friend. I may be a little late, but I shall surely come,” and Jo longs to see “my dear old Fritz.”

chapters.title: Surprises
chapters.intro: Background on unmarried women and chaperons in the nineteenth century, Samuel Johnson, Dickens, Aesop, Goethe and a well-known hymn, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: An unmarried woman, usually one past the usual age for marrying.
A short sermon or moral lecture.
To block a way with a barrier; also the barrier itself.
A lively, mischievous person who is always getting into scrapes.
An older woman who accompanies a young unmarried woman to keep her behavior proper.
The back of a horse’s leg just above the hoof, where a tuft of hair grows.
An official who looks after his own country’s citizens and business in a foreign city.
A chain worn at a lady’s waist with small useful things hanging from it, such as keys, scissors or a watch.
A promised future age of perfect happiness; loosely, a time of great joy.
Latin for “at pleasure”: as much as one likes.
A fine, thin white cloth of linen or cotton.
A soft woolen cloth made from the fleece of merino sheep.
A small closed carriage for two passengers, with a seat outside for the driver.
Fine lace made entirely with a needle.
French for “too much”: unwanted, one too many in company.

In the nineteenth century an unmarried woman past her mid-twenties was often called an old maid and was frequently pitied or mocked. Some writers defended single women, pointing to their usefulness and quiet sacrifices.
Respectable young unmarried women in society were expected to travel and go out with an older married woman. English and European society was generally stricter about this than American custom.
Well-off American families of the period often spent long stretches touring Europe, wintering in places such as Paris or on the Mediterranean coast.

In a famous 1755 letter to Lord Chesterfield, the English writer Samuel Johnson complained that help and praise had come too late: when he was indifferent and could not enjoy it, solitary and could not share it, known and did not need it.
Charles Dickens’s 1850 novel follows David from childhood to manhood. Peggotty, his loving and plainspoken nurse, is one of its best-loved characters.
The North Wind and the Sun
In Aesop’s fable the wind and the sun compete to make a traveler take off his cloak. The harder the wind blows, the tighter he holds it; the sun’s gentle warmth succeeds.

In Goethe’s novel Wilhelm Meister’s Apprenticeship, the girl Mignon sings “Know’st thou the land where the citron blooms?”, a song of longing for a warm southern country. Many composers set it to music.
A popular hymn with words by the Irish poet Thomas Moore, known for its line promising that earth has no sorrow that heaven cannot heal.
Educated people of the time enjoyed discussing how ancient peoples treated their dead: Greeks and Romans often burned bodies on a funeral pyre, while Egyptians embalmed them.
Berne, the Swiss capital, has a bear as its emblem, and carved wooden bears were a favorite souvenir for travelers to Switzerland.

quiz.q: As her birthday approaches, what does Jo expect to become?
o: A famous novelist with no time for a family
A literary spinster with a pen for a spouse
A governess for a rich family abroad
A teacher in a little school for girls
quiz.e: Almost twenty-five, Jo predicts “a literary spinster, with a pen for a spouse,” and a morsel of fame that comes too late, “like poor Johnson.”

quiz.q: How does Laurie give away his big news before he means to?
o: He hands Jo a letter signed by them both
He calls Mr. Laurence “our grandfather”
He says he is now the head of a family
He mentions “my wife” without thinking
quiz.e: He says Mrs. March has “my wife” down at Meg’s; the two words betray him, and Jo cries, “You’ve gone and got married!”

quiz.q: Why did Laurie and Amy decide to marry abroad instead of waiting?
o: Mrs. Carrol wouldn’t let Amy travel home without a chaperon
Aunt Carrol insisted on a grand wedding in Paris in the spring
Mr. Laurence was ill and wished to see Laurie settled at once
They feared the family would object if asked beforehand
quiz.e: The Carrols stayed in Paris, Mr. Laurence wanted to go home, and Mrs. Carrol’s “English notions about chaperons” kept Amy back, so Laurie said, “Let’s be married.”

quiz.q: Where did the couple spend their honeymoon?
o: In London
At Vevay
At Valrosa
In Heidelberg
quiz.e: Amy had once called Valrosa “a regular honeymoon home,” so they went there: “love among the roses.”

quiz.q: What does Jo say she and Laurie must be to each other from now on?
o: Partners in all their plans
Neighbors and nothing more
Playmates as in the old days
Brother and sister
quiz.e: Jo says playtime is over: “we will be brother and sister, to love and help one another all our lives.”

quiz.q: Which fable does Jo use to describe how Amy manages Laurie?
o: The tortoise and the hare
The sun and the wind
The lion and the mouse
The fox and the grapes
quiz.e: Jo says Amy is the sun and she was the wind, and “the sun managed the man best.” Laurie adds that Amy can blow him up as well as shine on him.

quiz.q: What does Mr. Laurence whisper to Jo as he takes her in to tea?
o: “You must be my girl now”
“Amy has done us all proud”
“Let us forget the past, my dear”
“You were right to refuse him”
quiz.e: With a glance at Beth’s empty corner he says “You must be my girl now,” and Jo answers, “I’ll try to fill her place, sir.”

quiz.q: What does Professor Bhaer notice when the hall light falls on Jo’s face?
o: That she has cut her hair short again
That she looks younger than in New York
That she looks changed, as if she had been ill
That she has been crying over a letter
quiz.e: He asks “You haf been ill, my friend?” and Jo says she is not ill, but tired and sorrowful.

quiz.q: When Laurie asks Amy to play for everyone, what does she do instead?
o: She plays a waltz she learned in Paris
She sings Beth’s songs, faltering on a hymn
She asks the Professor to play in her place
She shows everyone her sketches of Rome
quiz.e: Amy says she can’t show off tonight and sings Beth’s songs; her voice fails at the last line of Beth’s favorite hymn.

quiz.q: What seems to delight Professor Bhaer most just before he leaves?
o: Mr. March’s offer to lend him some of his books
An invitation to dine at Mr. Laurence’s house
Jo’s promise to sing Mignon’s song with him again
Learning that Amy, not Jo, is Laurie’s wife
quiz.e: Amy had been introduced only as “my sister”; when Laurie says “My wife and I,” the Professor looks “suddenly illuminated with satisfaction.”

chapters.title: My Lord and Lady
chapters.intro: Background on French society hostesses, old fables and ballads, Christian charity and its saints, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: A strong wish to have something that belongs to someone else.
A weather vane, often shaped like a rooster, that turns to show which way the wind blows.
A small, sudden shift or puff, as of the wind.
A device with a notched end for gripping the heel of a boot so it can be pulled off.
Teasing and amused, as if asking a playful question.
A regular gathering of writers, artists and notable people at a hostess’s home.
Informal: a thoroughly good, reliable person.
Very particular and hard to please.
Interested mainly in money or gain.
Someone who keeps others from having something he cannot use himself.
Of a person or family: fallen from wealth or rank into poverty.
Using smooth, flattering talk to get something.
Generous in helping others, especially with money.
To give a lasting fund of money to support an institution.
Money or property left to someone in a will.
Juliette Récamier (1777–1849) was a celebrated beauty whose Paris salon drew writers and politicians for decades. Her name became shorthand for a gracious society hostess.
The ancient Greek philosopher Aristotle wrote on ethics, politics, logic and nature, and was standard reading for scholars.
In an old fable a dog lies in a manger full of hay; it cannot eat the hay, yet it snarls to keep the hungry ox away.
An old English ballad tells of King Cophetua, who fell in love with a poor beggar girl and made her his queen. Tennyson and several painters later retold the story.

In the Bible (Acts 9), Dorcas, also called Tabitha, was a disciple “full of good works,” remembered for the garments she made for poor widows. Church sewing circles for the needy were often called Dorcas societies.
Martin of Tours, a fourth-century Roman soldier who later became a bishop, is said to have cut his cloak in half with his sword to share it with a freezing beggar.
Nineteenth-century writers often pitied educated families who had fallen on hard times: too proud to ask for charity, they often suffered more quietly than ordinary beggars.
Wealthy patrons had long supported struggling painters, sculptors and musicians, paying for training or for travel to study in Europe.
In New England, east winds blowing in off the Atlantic were known for being raw and damp, while westerly winds usually brought fairer weather.
The proverb “a new broom sweeps clean” means that newcomers start out full of energy and eager to make changes.

quiz.q: Why does Laurie come to borrow Amy from her mother the next day?
o: He can’t find something he wants in her luggage
His grandfather has asked to see her at once
Callers have come to the house hoping to see her
He wants her help in choosing new furniture
quiz.e: The luggage has come and he has been “making hay” of her Paris finery; Amy guesses he is hunting for his bootjack.

quiz.q: What does Laurie say he means to do once they are settled?
o: Study music seriously in Germany
Buy a farm and live in the country
Go into business, to delight his grandfather
Write a book about their travels
quiz.e: He means to “work like a man” to prove he isn’t spoilt: “I need something of the sort to keep me steady.”

quiz.q: What name does Laurie teasingly give Amy when describing her plans for society?
o: Queen Victoria
Madame Récamier
Lady Jane Grey
Madame de Staël
quiz.e: He jokes about the brilliant society she will gather; Amy privately resolves there will be a home with a good wife in it before any salon.

quiz.q: What is Laurie’s one reservation about Mr. Bhaer as a husband for Jo?
o: That he may take Jo away to Germany
That he is too grave and bookish for her
That he has two nephews to support
That he is not younger and richer
quiz.e: Laurie calls him “a trump” but wishes he were “a little younger and a good deal richer.”

quiz.q: Amy stops short in the middle of which remark?
o: That age matters little in a happy marriage
That women never should marry for money
That Jo deserves a much richer husband
That a wife should always rule her husband
quiz.e: She catches herself, remembering she once meant to make a rich match, and Laurie teases her about it with “malicious gravity.”

quiz.q: What does Amy say she is prouder of than of all Laurie’s money?
o: Her handsome husband himself
His kindness to her family
His new success in business
His fine baritone singing voice
quiz.e: She admires the dimple in his chin and confesses, “your nose is such a comfort to me.”

quiz.q: What plan does Laurie jokingly suggest for helping the Professor?
o: Giving him a post in his grandfather’s firm
Paying for the schooling of his two boys
Buying him a house near the Marches
Inventing a rich relation who leaves him money
quiz.e: Amy says Jo would find them out, since she is proud of him “just as he is”; they agree to watch for a chance to help.

quiz.q: Which people does Amy most want to help, remembering her own past?
o: Widows and orphans of the war
Poor gentlefolk too proud to ask for charity
Ambitious girls who need a little help
Sick children in the city hospitals
quiz.e: Amy says ambitious girls often see “youth, health, and precious opportunities go by” for want of help; Laurie calls her a Dorcas, and she calls him a St. Martin.

chapters.title: Daisy and Demi
chapters.intro: Background on Socrates, Dickens’s characters, American legends and nineteenth-century ideas about children, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: The age at which a person is thought old enough to judge and act sensibly.
A dining-room cabinet with cupboards and drawers for dishes and linen.
Someone forced to row a galley ship; loosely, anyone who does drudging work for another.
Long fixed in a habit and unlikely to change.
Showing abilities or behavior unusually early for one’s age.
A very wise person, often an old one.
The branch of philosophy that asks about the nature of being, mind and reality.
A rich boiled pudding made with dried fruit, suet and spices.
A small cake; also a clapping game played with small children.
A sleeveless, buttoned garment worn under a man’s coat; a vest.
Love of one’s children, or of children in general; a term from phrenology.
Someone lying flat on the ground, face down.
A hinged instrument with two pointed legs, used for drawing circles.
A cupboard for storing the good dishes.

Socrates, the Athenian philosopher of the fifth century BC, taught by asking question after question until his pupil reasoned out an answer, now called the Socratic method. Alcibiades, a brilliant, headstrong young Athenian, appears as his companion in Plato’s dialogues.
In Dickens’s Oliver Twist, the Artful Dodger is a quick-witted young pickpocket. His name came to describe any clever, slippery person who wriggles out of rules.
Sam Weller, the cheerful Cockney servant in Dickens’s The Pickwick Papers, swaps his v’s and w’s, so that “very” comes out “wery.”
A popular legend, spread by the early biographer Mason Locke Weems, has the boy George Washington confess to damaging his father’s cherry tree with the words “I cannot tell a lie.”
A Bible verse (Hebrews 13:2) urges kindness to strangers, “for thereby some have entertained angels unawares,” meaning without knowing it.
A favorite nursery rhyme about three kittens who lose their mittens, find them, soil them and wash them.

Phrenology, popular in the mid-1800s, claimed that bumps on the skull revealed a person’s talents and character, and gave long names to traits such as love of children. It has long since been discredited.
Rich puddings were often made well ahead of a holiday, tied in a cloth and boiled for hours in a large pot, and children were eager kitchen helpers for the raisins.
Small children usually learned the alphabet at home before school, from primers, blocks or picture cards, and inventive parents made a game of it.

quiz.q: What does Demi use as an “elevator” for his sister?
o: A pulley rigged to the nursery door
A wooden crate tied to a rope
A clothes basket on the stairs
A basket hung over a big chair
quiz.e: He tries to hoist Daisy in a basket hung over a chair: “Why, marmar, dat’s my lellywaiter, and me’s trying to pull her up.”

quiz.q: What does Daisy say each morning at the window, whatever the weather?
o: “Me loves evvybody!”
“Oh, pitty day!”
“Dood morning, sun!”
“Where’s my Dodo?”
quiz.e: It is “all fair weather in her world”: rain or shine, she says “Oh, pitty day, oh, pitty day!”

quiz.q: What does Daisy’s grandfather often call her?
o: “Beth”
“Little Meg”
“Sunshine”
“Marmee’s girl”
quiz.e: Meg hopes Daisy will bless the Dovecote as Beth blessed the old home, and Mr. March often calls her “Beth.”

quiz.q: When asked where he keeps his mind, what does Demi answer?
o: “In my head, like dranpa”
“In dranpa’s watch”
“In my little belly”
“Up in my bumps”
quiz.e: After standing on one leg like a stork, Demi says “In my little belly,” and his grandfather can only laugh and dismiss “the class in metaphysics.”

quiz.q: How does Demi outwit his mother on plum-pudding day?
o: He makes her promise anything, then asks for the raisins
He hides the raisins in his pinafore pocket
He coaxes Hannah into giving him the raisins
He trades his patty-cakes with Daisy for raisins
quiz.e: Meg promises to play anything they like, and Demi replies, “Then we’ll go and eat up all the raisins.”

quiz.q: Why does Demi decide not to resent “the bear-man” who takes Aunt Dodo’s attention?
o: The bear-man tells him stories about bears
The bear-man lets him ride high on his shoulders
The bear-man promises him a German toy
The bear-man has chocolate-drops and a watch
quiz.e: Demi hasn’t the heart to insult a rival with “a mine of chocolate-drops in his waistcoat-pocket” and a watch that can be freely shaken.

quiz.q: What is Mr. March doing when the Professor walks into the study?
o: Reading Plato aloud to Demi by the fire
Lying on the floor with his legs in the air
Building a toy steam engine with Demi
Writing a sermon at his old desk in the corner
quiz.e: He is teaching Demi the alphabet by forming letters with his legs; Demi makes a V and shouts “It’s a We, dranpa!”

quiz.q: Which question of Demi’s makes Mr. March realize why the Professor really calls?
o: “Why does ’Fessor always ask for dranpa?”
“Is the bear-man going to live here?”
“Do great boys like great girls, too?”
“Will Dodo go away with the bear-man?”
quiz.e: When Bhaer answers that they do sometimes, Mr. March glances at Jo’s retiring face with an idea “both sweet and sour.”

chapters.title: Under the Umbrella
chapters.intro: Background on shopping and street life in a nineteenth-century city, heraldry, German Americans and the American West, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.
