Household dishes and utensils made of silver or gold.
A design on a shield that serves as the emblem of a family.
A light, smooth cotton cloth used for linings; “twilled” silesia has a fine diagonal weave.
Cloth, thread, ribbon and similar goods, as sold in a dry-goods store.
The office of a merchant or business, where accounts are kept.
Flirting idly; here, roaming about in hope of meeting a sweetheart.
Here, a heavy horse-drawn wagon for carrying goods.
Shabby and falling apart from age or use.
Speed and efficiency in getting something done.
A rush basket used for packing figs or dates.
A large bottle with a narrow neck, usually in a wicker case.
A large horse-drawn public coach running along a fixed route.
Wet and bedraggled, with tails or skirts trailing in the mud.
City dry-goods stores sold cloth, ribbon, thread and trimmings. Needles came in small paper packets graded by number, with higher numbers meaning finer needles.
City streets of the period were crowded with horse-drawn wagons, carts and omnibuses, and in wet weather they turned to deep mud, especially hard on women’s long skirts.
Umbrellas of the time had heavy frames of whalebone or steel covered with silk or cotton, and a sturdy one was a valued and long-kept possession.
Rubber overshoes and boots, made practical by the invention of vulcanized rubber in the 1840s, were a welcome new comfort for walking in mud and slush.
A coat of arms identified a noble family. The bear and ragged staff, a bear chained to a knobbly pole, was the famous badge of the English Earls of Warwick.
Large numbers of Germans emigrated to the United States in the mid-1800s, among them scholars and teachers, and brought lively traditions of music, choral singing and the Christmas tree.
To New Englanders of the mid-1800s, “the West” usually meant the newer states beyond the Appalachians, such as Ohio, Illinois and Wisconsin, where many new colleges were being founded.
In the old fairy tale, a princess and her whole court sleep for a hundred years behind a hedge of thorns until a prince makes his way through the wood and wakes her.
In Catholic tradition a person officially declared a saint is said to be canonized, and objects connected with a saint are treasured as relics.

quiz.q: Where does Jo keep meeting the Professor on her evening walks?
o: On the bridge down by the river
On either path to Meg’s house
Outside Mr. Laurence’s gate
Near the post office in town
quiz.e: Though there are two paths to Meg’s, whichever she takes she meets him, and he never seems to see her until quite close.

quiz.q: What does Mrs. March ask Jo to do if she happens to meet Mr. Bhaer?
o: Bring him home to tea
Ask him to call on Sunday
Thank him for the books
Give him her best wishes
quiz.e: Mrs. March says she “quite longs to see the dear man,” and Jo kisses her, thinking “How good she is to me!”

quiz.q: Why does Jo end up among the warehouses and countinghouses?
o: She must buy paper at a stationer there
She has taken the wrong omnibus home
She hopes to run into the Professor there
She is taking a story to a publisher
quiz.e: She loiters near a warehouse marked “Hoffmann, Swartz, & Co.,” then scolds herself for “philandering down here, hoping to see the Professor.”

quiz.q: What news does the Professor give Jo about his future?
o: He is to write for a New York paper
He must go home to Germany for good
He will open a small school in the city
He has found a college post in the West
quiz.e: Friends have found him a place in a college “at the West,” where he can earn enough to help Franz and Emil. Jo cries “So far away!”

quiz.q: What favor does the Professor ask that makes Jo feel suddenly cool?
o: To carry a letter home to her father
To show him the way to the station
To help him buy a dress for his Tina
To choose a gift for her own mother
quiz.e: Jo expected something very different; he wants a little dress for Tina and a warm shawl for Tina’s poor, sick mother.

quiz.q: What does Jo answer when the Professor asks why she is crying?
o: “Because you are going away”
“I have a cold in my head”
“The rain is in my eyes”
“I have ruined my best bonnet”
quiz.e: Jo answers with a sob instead of a polite fib, and he cries “Ach, mein Gott, that is so good!” and asks for a little place in her heart.

quiz.q: What brought the Professor to Jo’s town at last?
o: A letter from Laurie telling him to come
News from Mr. March of the family’s loss
An invitation to lecture at a college
A lonely poem of hers he found in a paper
quiz.e: He found her verses “In the Garret” by chance and knew them by the names and initials; one verse “seemed to call me.”

quiz.q: Why must Jo and the Professor wait before they marry?
o: Jo has promised to keep house for Mr. Laurence
He must first keep his word to help his boys
Her parents wish them to wait three years
He must save enough to buy them a house
quiz.e: He must go West and work alone: “even for you, I may not break my word to Minna.” Jo says she has her own duty and work too.

chapters.title: Harvest Time
chapters.intro: Background on old writers about farming, Bible sayings, autumn harvest customs and nursery rhymes, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: Very long or large; filling many pages.
Of or like a stroke; also, so overcome by emotion as to seem about to burst.
A ragged, dirty child, especially a poor one.
Someone who spoils other people’s fun or enthusiasm.
An awkward, clumsy youth halfway between boy and man.
Extreme poverty; lacking even the basic needs of life.
The grounds or area within the boundaries of a place.
A collection of animals kept together.
An old term, now offensive, for a person with one Black grandparent.
A tall wildflower with plumes of small yellow flowers, blooming in late summer and fall.
A team of firefighters equipped with ladders and hooks.
Acrobatics done both on the ground and high in the air.
A kind of apple with rough, reddish-brown skin.
Embarrassed or put off one’s composure.
A bundle of grain stalks tied together after reaping.

Thomas Tusser wrote a popular sixteenth-century verse guide to farming, Five Hundred Points of Good Husbandry; Abraham Cowley was a seventeenth-century English poet who praised gardens and country life; Columella was a Roman author of a long work on agriculture.
Pomona was the Roman goddess of fruit trees and orchards, often shown with a basket of fruit or a pruning knife.
Henry Wadsworth Longfellow’s short 1842 poem “The Rainy Day” ends with the reminder that “into each life some rain must fall.”
This cumulative nursery rhyme includes “the cow with the crumpled horn” that tossed the dog that worried the cat.
In Jesus’s parable (Matthew 13), an enemy sows weeds called tares among a farmer’s wheat; the two grow together until harvest, when they are separated.
When Peter asks how often he must forgive, Jesus answers “seventy times seven” (Matthew 18), meaning without limit.
In Exodus, God promises the Israelites “a land flowing with milk and honey”; the phrase came to mean any place of plenty.
Autumn apple-picking was a busy time on New England farms, with whole families shaking the trees, gathering the fallen fruit and sorting it for eating, cider and storage.
At celebrations it was customary to drink toasts to honored guests and absent friends. “Three times three” meant three rounds of three cheers each.
The English bat-and-ball game was played in America in the mid-1800s, before baseball overtook it in popularity.
To build castles in the air is to daydream about an imagined future life.

quiz.q: What does Aunt March leave to Jo?
o: Her diamonds
Her library
Plumfield
Her parrot
quiz.e: Aunt March dies suddenly and leaves Plumfield to Jo, “which made all sorts of joyful things possible.”

quiz.q: What “crop” does Jo plan to raise at Plumfield?
o: Apples
Wheat
Roses
Boys
quiz.e: She plans “a good, happy, homelike school” for little lads, with herself to care for them and Fritz to teach them.

quiz.q: Whom does Jo hold up as proof that she has already raised one boy well?
o: Demi
Laurie
Tommy Bangs
Franz
quiz.e: She praises Teddy as “a steady, sensible business man” and says she will point to him: “There’s your model, my lads.”

quiz.q: How does Mr. Laurence help the school without hurting Jo’s pride?
o: He finds needy boys and pays a little for each
He quietly buys all the school’s books
He sends his own cook out to Plumfield
He lends Fritz money to mend the house
quiz.e: He keeps finding “some touching case of destitution” and offers to pay a trifle, giving Jo the poor boys she most delights in.

quiz.q: What name does Laurie suggest for the school?
o: “Jo’s Boys’ Home”
“Plumfield Academy”
“Mother Bhaer’s”
“The Bhaer-garten”
quiz.e: He calls it the “Bhaer-garten,” as a compliment to its master and appropriate to its inhabitants.

quiz.q: What are Jo’s own two sons named?
o: Fritz and Laurie
Rob and Teddy
John and Demi
Franz and Emil
quiz.e: Rob is named for grandpa, and Teddy is a happy-go-lucky baby with his papa’s sunny temper and his mother’s lively spirit.

quiz.q: What is the first toast at the apple-picking supper?
o: “Aunt March, God bless her!”
“To Mother Bhaer’s boys!”
“To the memory of Beth!”
“Long life to Mr. Laurence!”
quiz.e: The Professor never forgets how much he owes her, and the boys are taught to keep her memory green; next comes grandma’s sixtieth birthday.

quiz.q: What is the one shadow over Amy’s happiness?
o: Laurie’s long absences on business
Her failure to finish her statue
The frail health of her little daughter
A coolness with Mr. Laurence
quiz.e: Her daughter Beth is a frail little creature, and the fear of losing her binds Amy and Laurie closely together.
